item.title: Red, orange, yellow or green? How bell pepper colors reveal different health benefits
item.description: Click here for more articles by Kormedi.com. Bell peppers do more than add vibrant colors and a satisfying crunch to dishes such as salads and japchae, a Korean stir-fried glass noodle dish. Their colors also offer clues to the nutrients they contain, with each variety providing different nutritional benefits. From vitamin A precursors that support vision in dim light to compounds that help protect the retina and vitamin C that improves iron absorption, the nutritional profiles of bell peppers vary depending on their color. So which color should you choose, and how can you get the most out of its nutrients? Red bell peppers: Beta-carotene supports vision in low light Red bell peppers are rich in beta-carotene, a pigment that the body can convert into vitamin A. According to comparative data released by Korea's Rural Development Administration, red bell peppers had the highest beta-carotene content among the four colors examined. item.title: Why Korean occult films are casting a spell on audiences in Vietnam and Indonesia
item.description: Korean occult thriller "Exhuma" (2024) was a massive box-office success at home, drawing nearly 12 million moviegoers. But its remarkable performance in Vietnam and Indonesia, where it broke records previously held by other Korean films, revealed something equally significant: Southeast Asia could become a lucrative market for Korean supernatural cinema. The film, which explores feng shui, shamanism, ancestral graves and the legacy of Japanese colonial rule, struck a chord with audiences in countries where spiritual traditions remain deeply rooted and horror is already a popular genre. Its success has also attracted the attention of Korean film producers and investors searching for new opportunities overseas as the domestic theatrical market struggles to recover from a prolonged downturn. 'Exhuma' breaks records at home and abroad "Exhuma" was produced on a budget of 14 billion won ($9.4 million). item.title: Impeachment motion against Supreme Court chief likely to be initiated on 2nd anniversary of martial law bid: lawmaker
item.description: The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) is expected to initiate a parliamentary motion to impeach the Supreme Court chief justice on Dec. 3, the second anniversary of ousted former President Yoon Suk Yeol's 2024 martial law bid, the party's spokesman said Saturday. Rep. Cho Gye-won, the spokesman, made the remark a day after the DPK made an official decision to seek the impeachment of Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae over its accusation that the top court complied with Yoon's martial law declaration, its decision to send President Lee Jae Myung's election law case back to the appeals court and other reasons. Though no official decision or discussions have been made, Rep. Cho said there appears to be a tacit "consensus" in the party about initiating the motion on Dec. 3, a point in time that he said can "demonstrate a firm determination to root out the insurrection."

item.title: Rights commission to recommend IFEZ stop excluding foreign residents from bridge toll exemption
item.description: The rights watchdog is set to recommend that the Incheon Free Economic Zone (IFEZ) Authority revise a toll exemption program for the Cheongna Sky Bridge, as the current rule excluding foreign residents of Incheon from the program discriminates against them. According to a draft of the National Human Rights Commission of Korea's recommendation obtained exclusively by The Korea Times on Saturday, the commission found little reasonable basis for the exclusion, calling it "a discriminatory act violating the right to equality." “Given that the bridge toll exemption program aims to ease local residents’ transportation burden and improve their living conditions, it is hard to see a reasonable justification for excluding foreign residents solely on the formal ground that they are not subject to resident registration,” the commission said in the draft. It added that, besides the resident registration for locals, there are other means through which foreign residents can have their residence in Incheon officially verified. item.title: Lee visits AI data center construction site in Ulsan
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung visited an artificial intelligence (AI) data center construction site in the southern port city of Ulsan on Saturday, a day after he concluded a four-day trip to the Philippines and China. The visit was aimed at checking the progress of the government-led "mega projects" aimed at transforming three regional provinces -- the central region of Chungcheong, the southwestern region of Honam and the southern region of Yeongnam -- into hubs for cutting-edge industries, such as AI data centers, physical AI and advanced semiconductors. "AI data centers are a major source of demand for semiconductors and key infrastructure behind physical AI, such as robots and autonomous vehicles," Lee said as he toured the construction site of an AI data center operated by SK. "I expect the successful progress of the AI data center project in Ulsan will serve as a catalyst for additional investments from global AI companies," he added. item.title: A 24-year-old Korean's Silicon Valley gamble pays off with a16z backing
item.description: Lee Seung-heon, also known as Heon Lee in the U.S., has chosen a path that many other Koreans would consider too risky to take. He dropped out of college to work full time at Philyron, a San Francisco-based maritime technology startup he co-founded in June this year. “Korean students and their parents feel pressure when it comes to choosing a career over a college education. But in Silicon Valley, I’ve met plenty of young Americans who dropped out of prestigious universities to start their own businesses,” he told The Korea Times. “There is certainly a cultural difference between the two countries when it comes to college education. I concluded that starting my own business was the right decision and that spending three more years in college would be meaningless because schools don’t teach you how to start a business and keep it growing.” Lee, 24, initially studied political science at Boston University. item.title: Art becomes key component of financial services for wealthy clients
item.description: Art is finding a place in the world of personalized wealth management, as Korea’s financial firms look beyond traditional services to cater to the interests and lifestyles of their wealthy clients, according to industry watchers on Friday. For years, private banking revolved around investment products, tax planning and inheritance. Now, banks and insurers are adding art to the mix, betting that helping clients navigate the art world can give them an edge in the competitive business of managing the wealthy. The appeal is reflected in the numbers. Art accounted for an average of 15 percent of high-net-worth collectors’ overall wealth portfolios this year, according to the Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026. They spent an average of $124,265 on fine art in 2025, 13 percent more than a year earlier. In Korea, collecting is starting to draw interest not only as a matter of taste but also as a way to manage and pass on wealth. “People with money often get into art through their social circles. item.title: From online mockery to addictive drama: 'The Remarried Empress' wins over viewers as finale nears
item.description: What began as a wave of online ridicule over questionable styling and unusual visuals is turning into growing enthusiasm for Disney+'s Korean fantasy romance "The Remarried Empress," as its fast-paced plot, tangled relationships and increasingly intense performances draw viewers deeper into the story. The Disney+ series released its seventh and eighth episodes on Wednesday, bringing the troubled marriage between Emperor Sovieshu (Ju Ji-hoon) and Empress Navier (Shin Min-a) closer to collapse. In the latest episodes, Sovieshu decides to divorce Navier, sending their already strained relationship into a downward spiral as the 10-part series approaches its conclusion. Based on a popular Korean web novel and webtoon, "The Remarried Empress" follows Navier, the seemingly perfect empress of the Eastern Empire, whose husband falls for Rashta (Lee Se-young), an escaped slave. When Sovieshu seeks a divorce, Navier agrees on one condition: that he approve her remarriage to Heinrey (Lee Jong-suk), a prince of the Western Kingdom. item.title: Veteran actress criticizes younger actors but recalls why Park Bo-gum stood out
item.description: Veteran actress Bae Jong-ok, known for her blunt criticism of younger actors' attitudes on set, has once again taken aim at those who spend too much time in their vehicles instead of preparing for scenes. Yet her past praise for actor Park Bo-gum, who once became so emotional that he cried before the cameras even started rolling, offers a striking contrast. Bae criticized the work habits of some younger actors during a press screening for her film "A Perfect Home" at CGV Yongsan I'Park Mall in Seoul on Wednesday. "Jang Gyu-ri and Kim Min-chul weren't like that, but sometimes when I visit sets, I wonder if young actors have honey smeared all over their cars because they never seem to leave them," Bae said. "They stay in their cars until right before filming, and only come out when the staff tell them they have to start shooting. Sometimes I even ask younger actors, 'Is there something stuck to your car?' It's really frustrating to watch." item.title: NewJeans' Haerin steps into spotlight again as other members remain largely out of sight
item.description: Haerin of K-pop girl group NewJeans is emerging as the group's most publicly active member following her return to agency Ador, making her second official appearance in two months while her bandmates have largely stayed out of the spotlight. On Friday, Haerin attended a photo call for a cosmetics brand at Shinsegae Department Store's Gangnam branch in southern Seoul, drawing attention with her elegant styling and signature catlike features. The singer wore a black dress featuring a ribbon detail at the waist, paired with a distinctive clutch from luxury fashion house Dior. Her large eyes, delicate facial features and subtle smile gave her a doll-like appearance, combining an innocent charm with an air of mystery. Haerin waved to cameras and posed with finger hearts pressed against her cheeks, showing a playful side during the event. item.title: Actor Kim Min turns real-life hero as he helps battle rapidly spreading wildfire
item.description: Actor Kim Min helped contain a rapidly spreading wildfire in Gangwon Province, risking his own safety as flames scorched his jacket during an emergency firefighting effort. According to JTBC on Friday, Kim spotted a fire in Goseong, Gangwon Province, on Thursday while returning to his accommodation after filming the upcoming Netflix series "The Twilight Between Us." Kim initially planned to report the fire and continue to his accommodation. But when he saw how quickly the flames were spreading, he stopped his vehicle and rushed to the scene to help extinguish them. The fire reportedly grew from about 16 square meters to roughly 165 square meters in just five minutes. With strong winds blowing from a nearby resort toward the mountains, there were concerns that the blaze could develop into a major wildfire. Kim joined a resort employee in tackling the flames with fire extinguishers available at the building, helping prevent the fire from spreading further. item.title: Trump says 'confronting dangers on Korean Peninsula' discussed at 3-way summit with Xi, Putin
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that "confronting dangers" on the Korean Peninsula was discussed when he held three-way summit talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin this week. "We also talked about confronting dangers on the Korean Peninsula and stopping the killing in Ukraine," Trump said during a press conference at the White House. He did not elaborate on what the "dangers on the Korean Peninsula" mean. The historic talks took place Thursday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.

item.title: Freight train derails near Sejong, leaving Saemaeul, Mugunghwa services suspended
item.description: PYEONGTAEK/SEJONG — Five cars of a freight train derailed near the central administrative city of Sejong early Saturday, leaving Saemaeul and Mugunghwa train services between the cities of Daejeon and Cheonan suspended. High-speed KTX services were unaffected, and no human casualties were reported. The 21-car train went off the rails after an automatic emergency brake system activated as it entered Sojeong-ri Station in Sejong, some 120 kilometers south of Seoul, at 5:37 a.m. When the train went off the tracks, it hit and broke a steel support pole, snapping the overhead power lines and causing a power outage between Cheonan and Jeonui stations. The accident initially delayed Saemaeul and Mugunghwa passenger trains before services were suspended. KTX bullet trains, which run on separate tracks, were not affected. Korea Railroad Corp. (KORAIL) said it will use buses to transport passengers over the suspended section so that they can change trains to their ultimate destinations. item.title: Araqchi says Iran wants diplomacy to end war; Trump says terms unacceptable
item.description: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its war with the United States, while US President Donald Trump said Iran wanted a deal but one that was not acceptable to him. Araqchi told the state-owned Iran newspaper that Tehran was seeking "an agreement that would ensure there was no further war" and wanted guarantees that Washington was serious about negotiations before proceeding further, adding that Iran had discussed with mediators the form and nature of confidence-building measures. The remarks came as diplomatic efforts continued to try to end a conflict that has destabilized the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices and drawn in countries across the region. The foreign minister said Iran's red lines included keeping enriched uranium in the country, though he added that he believed "a fair solution" could be reached. "They want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me," Trump said at a press conference on Friday. item.title: Texas prisoner moans in pain for minutes during unusual lethal injection, witnesses say
item.description: A condemned Texas prisoner moaned and yelled out in pain and remained conscious for several minutes after prison officials began administering lethal injections in what witnesses described on Friday as an unusually protracted execution. Prison officials took about 34 minutes to successfully insert two intravenous lines in convicted murderer Reinaldo Dennes: one in his neck and the other in his left foot after the veins in his arms were found unviable, according to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. They began injecting pentobarbital, a caustic barbiturate, at 6:52 p.m. on Thursday, and he was declared dead 15 minutes later, according to the department's records, during which a media witness and a spiritual adviser said Dennes repeatedly moaned in pain. The spiritual adviser, the Rev. Jeff Hood, recalled Dennes using repeated expletives and saying: "My leg is killing me," and, "My leg it's on fire, it's on fire." "He was clearly in tremendous distress," Hood, who was inside the execution chamber with his hand on Dennes' shoulder, told reporters. "Twice he said 'it's not working, it

item.title: Telecoms ramp up AI investment amid questions over returns
item.description: Major telecom companies are increasing capital expenditures as they expand into artificial intelligence (AI) data center businesses, with questions remaining over their ability to recoup the growing investments as construction and operating costs mount. According to the companies' regulatory filings on Friday, SK Telecom, KT and LG Uplus spent a total of 3.68 trillion won ($2.75 billion) on capital expenditure in the first nine months of this year, up 13.7 percent from a year earlier. LG Uplus posted the biggest increase, with capital expenditure on a standalone basis reaching 569.8 billion won in the third quarter, up 30.1 percent year-on-year. The increase was largely driven by investment in its AI data center project in Paju, Gyeonggi Province. The company is building a 200-megawatt-scale facility in the city, with four buildings scheduled to begin operations by 2028. Its first 50-megawatt building is expected to be completed by next June, while the company says it has secured customer demand for all four buildings. item.title: Robots patrol parks, serve meals in Seoul's wealthy Gangnam District
item.description: In Seoul’s affluent Gangnam District, long synonymous with glittering skyscrapers, luxury boutiques and K-pop glamour, the newest public servants roll on wheels, purify library air and strap onto the backs of sanitation workers. Under an expanded municipal trial unveiled recently, Gangnam District is deploying artificial intelligence (AI)-powered robots across five everyday civic roles — patrolling parks for fire hazards, clearing lunch trays at a senior center and assisting street sweepers with heavy lifting. The program transforms the bustling urban district into a live testing ground for Korean robotics startups eager to prove their machines can survive the unpredictability of real city streets. The initiative underscores a wider national push across Korea, which already leads the world in industrial robot density — with more than 1,000 robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers — and is now racing to bring automation out of factories and into daily life. item.title: Mexican novelist explores Korea through AI dolls, shamans, beauty in 'Peeling'
item.description: Beyond the global appeal of K-pop, K-dramas and K-beauty lies another side of Korea. For Mexican anthropologist and novelist Verónica González Laporte, who lived in Seoul for more than five years with her husband, former Mexican Ambassador to Korea Bruno Figueroa Fischer, her affection for the country inspired her to look beyond its polished image and explore the complexities of a society where cutting-edge technology coexists with centuries-old beliefs. "I was trying to offer another Korea, as I always try to go behind the stage," González told The Korea Times, explaining the inspiration behind her latest novel, "Peeling," which explores Korean society through the intertwined themes of beauty, isolation, gender and shamanism. From real-life encounters to fiction The novel follows Ji-ho, a plastic surgeon who, after a series of failed relationships and a period of loneliness, orders an AI sex doll named Seong-mi and falls in love with her. As he grows increasingly attached to the doll, his father becomes critically ill. A shaman warns that his father's condition is linked to a family

item.title: Nvidia's accounting is focus of US SEC investigation, sources say
item.description: NEW YORK/WASHINGTON — The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant. The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company. A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog is examining. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action. item.title: Former Nvidia CEO Huang agreed to testify at public US Senate hearing, senator's aide says
item.description: WASHINGTON — Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the U.S. Senate in a public hearing, an aide to Republican U.S. Senator Tim Scott said in a statement on Friday, as lawmakers probe allegations about Huang's ties to a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Huang has drawn increased attention from U.S. lawmakers since the New York Times reported he had a romantic relationship with the woman, raising questions on exports of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China. If the hearing proceeds as planned, it would mark Huang's first public testimony since stepping down as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12. A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment on the hearing. Scott's office did not provide a date, though the senator's original request asked Huang to appear on December 3. Huang separately agreed to a closed-door interview with three House committees, slated for December 1.

item.title: Trump calls for Nvidia's Huang to be given 'second chance'
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday called for chip giant Nvidia to reinstate disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang after he resigned over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. "I would love to see him be back. You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?" Trump told reporters. "I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance." Huang resigned last week as chief of Nvidia, a company at the center of the AI revolution, after revelations of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funneled restricted chips to that country. Reports of at least two further affairs emerged after that initial report, with U.S. intelligence said to be aware of the possibility of the alleged Chinese espionage. Trump defended Huang as "a good man" who "made some bad decisions." item.title: Trump defends calling Putin a friend, unsure if he's a friend to US
item.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has defended calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a friend but says he “can’t speak” to whether the Russian leader is a friend to the U.S. Trump raised eyebrows in China days ago with his warm welcome and repeated references to his Russian counterpart as his “friend,” and he did not back away from that in the briefing room on Friday. item.title: Trump vows 'tremendous tax' for US firms building data centers in other countries
item.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries. Trump did not provide details Friday and he said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms. Trump says, “You ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off.” With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses. item.title: Fed's Cook says rate hikes needed to lower high inflation
item.description: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook on Friday made a case for more interest rate hikes, saying the U.S. central bank's current policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels she views with "great concern." "In a different environment, the (Federal Open Market) Committee could afford to be patient, but I continue to believe that in this economic climate we do not have that luxury," given how high inflation is and for how long it has been above the Fed's 2 percent target, Cook said in the text of a speech to be presented at a central bank conference in Chile. Cook said the quarter-percentage-point rate hike the Fed delivered at its September 15-16 policy meeting was not enough to moderate current levels of inflation. What's more, "inflation data received since the September rate increase, including reports last week, fail to provide me with sufficient evidence that inflation is returning to a sustainable path," she said. "There is little evidence inflation is declining." Cook, who voted for a rate hike at that meeting, was one of two Fed officials who dissented over the Fed's

item.title: Anthropic's post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
item.description: Anthropic's much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Friday as a dramatic unraveling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. As the first large machine-learning model maker to go public, Anthropic is widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, and its listing had been viewed as a potential boost for a sector struggling to regain its footing. But the stock was last trading at $87.28, about 10 percent below Thursday's close and not far from its $83 IPO price, while declines in other technology heavyweights suggested the listing had done little to stem the broader selloff. "Anthropic faded relatively quickly. I don't think investors believe there's something inherently wrong with the company, management or business. I think they're just skeptical of this market," said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth. The AI boom has come under pressure over the past month as concerns mount that spending on the technology, expected by some estimates to top $1 trillion this year, is not generating returns quickly e

item.title: Second judge blocks Trump's triumphal arch, calling it a 'rushed job'
item.description: ALEXANDRIA, Virginia — A federal judge on Friday blocked construction of President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch, saying it was a “rushed job” that lacked a legal basis. During a court hearing, U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, said she would issue an injunction indefinitely blocking the proposed 250-foot (76-meter) arch near Arlington National Cemetery from moving forward while she hears a legal challenge brought by Virginia's Arlington County. A different judge in Washington had previously blocked the project until December 3 and is weighing a longer-term injunction. Brinkema, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, said there were multiple defects in the federal government’s analysis of the economic and environmental impact of the project, including an inadequate explanation of how it will affect nearby Reagan Washington National Airport. "That just hasn’t been done in the case because it’s been such a rushed job,” the judge said. The ruling was the latest courtroom setback for one of Trump's many efforts to leave a lasting architectu

item.title: Trump faces tumult at home after Xi-Putin 'embarrassment'
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump returned to face post-midterms turmoil at home Friday after strutting on the world stage in a widely criticized meeting in China with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Trump was holding a press conference at the White House at noon (1700 GMT) on what he said was a "Great and Highly Consequential Trip" to Shenzhen and Manila. But U.S. media and Trump's opponents dismissed his trilateral summit as a little more than a photo opportunity for a lame-duck president seeking to reassert some power abroad. Trump was mocked in particular for saying "that's my friend" as he greeted Russia's Putin, despite Moscow's brutal war in Ukraine. The news conference will be a chance for Trump to try to reset the narrative by talking up his trip and its benefits for the United States, with the Republican saying he will also be discussing trade deals with Asian nations. item.title: Trump, Xi did not discuss Nvidia's Huang: US Treasury Secretary
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump did not discuss former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday. Huang resigned as chief of the chip giant at the center of the artificial intelligence revolution after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funneled restricted chips to that country. Responding to a question, Bessent told U.S. broadcaster CNBC that Huang had not come up in Trump's talks with Xi, held earlier this week in Shenzhen. item.title: Signal restricts screenshots to block AI agents from reading messages
item.description: NEW YORK — Encrypted messaging service Signal said on Friday it would restrict screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats on phones, warning that the tech industry's push to embed AI in consumer devices was eroding its ability to guarantee privacy. Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly. The move reflects growing tension between privacy-focused apps and the biggest tech companies, which are racing to roll out AI agents designed to see what is on a user's screen and take actions based on it. Signal identified as particularly worrisome the AI capabilities built directly into operating systems, like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligen

item.title: Bessent says still living at US military base, vows to squeeze Iran
item.description: WASHINGTON — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday he was still living at a U.S. military base after receiving unspecified threats from Iran, but vowed to continue squeezing the country economically. "If the Iranians are after me, it means that they are being squeezed. We're going to continue squeezing them," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC. Treasury has been tightening sanctions on Iran. The U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February and the conflict is simmering in the region despite intermittent talks on a resolution.

item.title: Nasdaq falls as Anthropic fails to rekindle AI optimism
item.description: Tumbling technology-related shares led a global stock selloff on Friday, with U.S. traders rotating into defensive sectors and the U.S. 10-year yield dropping by the most in a month. Stock benchmarks in Japan and Korea tumbled over 5 percent overnight to close the week, while on Wall Street chipmaker shares were down close to 6 percent. Taiwanese shares were down 17 percent for the week, their biggest weekly decline since 1990. Anthropic fell as much as 12.5 percent on its first full day of trading. Consumer staples and healthcare led sector gains on the S&P 500, which was still on track to post its largest weekly loss since March 2025. "Markets are entering a more defensive phase," said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com. "Strong AI demand and successful individual listings are no longer sufficient to sustain broader risk appetite when investors are questioning valuations, borrowing costs and the outlook for corporate profitability." The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.08 percent to 49,135.56, the S&P 500 fell 1.20 percent to 7,089.64 and the Nasdaq Composite fell

item.title: Celebrities' YouTube channels become double-edged sword
item.description: It is the age of self-promotion. Celebrities are increasingly turning to their own channels, beyond their acting projects and television appearances, to communicate with the public and reveal different sides of themselves. From behind-the-scenes footage of their work to glimpses of their everyday lives in private spaces, they are making efforts to bring themselves closer to their audiences. For stars, approachability has become a new competitive advantage and a way to win public favor. But as the distance between celebrities and their fans narrows, unexpected controversies are also becoming more common. Attempts to connect with audiences through an image of familiarity are increasingly turning into sources of controversy. Actress Son Tae-young recently found herself at the center of a heated debate over remarks she made on her YouTube channel. item.title: Love, conflict and the paradox of choice: Inside Korea's dating show boom
item.description: At a park along the Skagit Riverwalk in Mount Vernon, Washington, a man in a white dress shirt sat on a bench, holding three tulips. He was waiting for his “wife.” She traveled from Busan to Incheon International Airport before embarking on an 11-hour flight to the United States, barely sleeping at all during the journey. “Are you hungry? Are you? This is so awkward.” When she finally arrived, he appeared flustered and unsure of what to say. There was a good reason for his awkwardness: It was the first time the two had ever met. The man was Sang-cheol, a contestant on the 16th season of the dating reality show “I Am Solo,” and the woman was Young-sook, a contestant from its 28th season. The two recently began living together as a married couple on “Marriage of Convenience,” a reality show released on KBS Joy, MBC every1 and Netflix. The premise is that a man and a woman first live together as if they were married before deciding whether to actually tie the knot. Neither Sang-cheol nor Young-sook knew they would be paired with each other. Nam Gyu-hong, the producer oversee

item.title: ASCC-SGA hosts Fall 2026 Career Fair
item.description:
By 
James Kneubuhl, ASCC Press Officer

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA  — The Student Government Association (SGA) at the American Samoa Community College (ASCC) hosted its fall 2026 Career Fair on Tuesday, November 9th. With this event, the SGA assists students seeking local and federal opportunities to begin a career or looking for internships and summer jobs. 

Now a regular event every spring and fall semester at ASCC, the Career Fair typically features representatives from more than a dozen businesses and other organizations in the public and private sector meeting one-on-one with students to inform them of available opportunities along with any requirements involved. This semester, the SGA recorded 146 students taking part in the two-hour event, which took place in the College’s Multi-Purpose Center auditorium.

SGA Coordinator Ms. Falaileato Suiaunoa explained that more than a month of preparation goes into the Career Fair. 

“As a group, the SGA deliberates on which departments, businesses and organizations we invite. Our SGA President is involved in creating an invitation letter and gathering information. Invitation letters usually go out four to six weeks in advance, after which we follow-up regularly. On the day of the event, we maintain constant contact with all the vendors that come. Hosting the Career Fair provides a valuable opportunity for the SGA to develop their leadership, communication and collaboration skills.”

Asked about the effectiveness of the Career Fair, Ms. Suiaunoa described feedback received from participating businesses and agencies as “very positive and helpful.” 

As she explained, “We have had students set up job interviews and even secure positions as a result of the Career Fair. We just recently began the survey process with our vendors and agencies, but the earliest results indicate the Career Fair definitely helps employers and students connect. Also, since we began utilizing our ASG Human Resources and programs like WIOA, these entities have been very helpful in assisting our students with summer jobs.” 

Participants in this semester’s ASCC Career Fair included the American Samoa Visitors Bureau; Department of Human and Social Services; Public Works; the National Parks; American Samoa Legal Aid; American Samoa Telecommunications Authority; the US Army- 9th Mission Support Command; Utah National Guard; Back on Track; PIOA Consulting and Engineering; ASCC Teacher Education Department and Lumana’i Educators Association; American Samoa Human Resources/ Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act; Bluesky; US Marine Corps; Department of Homeland Security; American Samoa Democratic Party; ASCC Human Resources; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association; and the Christopher James Foeoletini Ledoux Foundation.

For more information on the American Samoa Community College and its many opportunities and services, visit the College’s website at: www.amsamoa.edu.

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
ASCC Career Fair

item.title: Owner of Continental Transport Corporation expresses frustration with location setbacks
item.description:
Says its not only with Zoning Board, but also with Industrial Park management
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — For more than three decades, Continental Transport Corporation (CTC) has been a familiar name in American Samoa's construction industry, supplying building materials and providing services that support both government and private-sector projects. Today, however, the company finds itself at a crossroads.

After being denied permission twice by the American Samoa Zoning Board to relocate its retail and production operations, CTC owner Tony Togia'i says he is running out of options. 

Frustrated by the repeated setbacks, Togia'i is now faced with the challenge of finding a suitable location where his company can resume full operations, continue serving customers, and generate enough revenue to pay employees, meet financial obligations, and keep the business afloat.

The CTC owner complained that their predicament is especially frustrating given his company's long service to the territory's development and infrastructure needs since the mid-1990s. 

For more than a decade, CTC operated from its production and retail headquarters in Fogagogo near Maliu Mai Beach Resort, where it supplied construction materials and provided a range of services to contractors, homeowners, and government agencies. That chapter came to an end in 2025 when the company's lease expired and was not renewed.

Following the loss of its Fogagogo facility, Togia'i sought alternative locations that could accommodate CTC's extensive operations. Among the options pursued was space at the government-owned Senator Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park in Tafuna.

Togia'i recalled that he had previously approached local businessman and Tool Shop owner Peter Crispin about the possibility of subleasing the last lot on the street near the turnoff adjacent to NAPA Auto Parts and across from the Department of Public Works (DPW) compound. The property had previously been occupied by an ice manufacturing company, and Crispin had acquired the lease from the former operators. According to Togia'i, Crispin was receptive to the proposal and indicated that he would consider the request and get back to him. However, he never received a response.

Seeking other options, Togia'i turned to Uili Leauanae, Deputy Director of the Department of Commerce (DOC). He said Leauanae informed him that there were no available lots within the Industrial Park that could accommodate the company's needs, leaving CTC with limited alternatives for relocating its operations.

Leauanae subsequently advised him that three vacant one-acre government lots were available for lease in the Vailoa-Leone area commonly known as the "Airstrip," and suggested that the company pursue the necessary approvals to secure one of the sites. According to Togia'i, Leauanae advised him to apply for a zoning variance and pursue a government lease for the property.

The area derives its nickname from the former Leone Airfield, a World War II-era military airstrip constructed by the U.S. Navy. The airfield once encompassed what are now several well-known landmarks, including Leone High School, Midkiff Elementary School, and the site of the former WVUV 648- AM radio station. Although the airfield was abandoned in early 1945 because of turbulent wind conditions and limited operational use, the area continues to be popularly known as the "Airstrip."

However, the proposal encountered strong opposition from nearby residents, who argued that the operation would pose significant environmental risks and potentially endanger public health and safety, particularly for students attending the two neighboring public schools. Their concerns ultimately played a major role in the Zoning Board's decision to deny CTC's application for a zoning variance.

The company's most recent setback came earlier this month when the Zoning Board again rejected a variance application, this time for a proposed site in Tula on communal land belonging to CTC owner Tony Togia'i's family. 

The denial followed objections raised by a resident whose home is located downwind of the proposed facility. Togia'i noted that he had submitted a petition supporting the project that was signed by several residents living near the proposed site, but the board ultimately sided with the concerns raised by the opposing resident.

A frustrated Togia'i told Samoa News that he felt his predicament was unfair. He said he fully understood why the Zoning Board denied his application for a zoning variance at the Airstrip site in Vailoa, given its close proximity to homes, schools, and government facilities. He noted that several residents had submitted written objections, while others appeared in person at the board's public hearing to voice their concerns.

However, Togia'i argued that the board's decision to reject his most recent application for a brick-manufacturing facility on his family's communal land in Tula was far more difficult to understand. He pointed out that the denial was based largely on the objection of a single resident whose home was not located in the immediate vicinity of the proposed site.

According to Togia'i, the board gave greater weight to that opposition than to a petition supporting the project that had been signed by several residents whose homes are adjacent to the proposed location. He said those residents would be the most directly affected by the operation and had no objection to the project moving forward. He stated that he was going to submit a request for reconsideration to the Zoning Board.

The disgruntled CTC owner said he has already invested heavily in the venture and must now begin searching for yet another suitable location. He estimated that he has spent approximately $50,000 on state-of-the-art equipment for the manufacture of concrete bricks and tri-bars, large reinforced concrete structures commonly used as wave breakers and shoreline protection barriers to help control coastal erosion and safeguard infrastructure from storm-driven waves.

"I've tried every available option that was suggested to me, but each one has led to another dead end," Togia'i said. "Now I have to start all over again looking for a place where I can operate."

Togia'i said he was particularly disappointed by the board's decision because CTC is one of only two local companies manufacturing concrete bricks in the Territory, the other being CBT/ Builders Hub.

According to Togia'i, major hardware retailers such as Ace Hardware and Tool Shop currently import much of their brick supply from Fiji. He said CTC's bricks were sent to Fiji for independent quality testing and exceeded the required standards.

The favorable test results, he added, led Ace Hardware to enter into a special arrangement with CTC under which the company would serve as Ace's exclusive local supplier of concrete bricks.

Togia'i argued that supporting local manufacturing would help reduce reliance on imported construction materials while creating economic opportunities within the Territory. He noted that CTC had already invested heavily in equipment and production capabilities in anticipation of growing demand for locally made bricks and other concrete products.

The CTC owner also expressed frustration with what he described as the government's management of the Senator Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park. Togia'i argued that greater priority should be given to local manufacturing and construction companies such as CTC, which he said has spent more than five decades serving the people of American Samoa and contributing to the Territory's economy.

Instead, he claimed that industrial park lots are often awarded to high-ranking government officials, their relatives, and businesses from outside the Territory, while established local companies struggle to secure suitable sites for expansion.

"Surely more than 50 years of service and contributing to the Territory's economy should mean something," a disappointed Togia'i said. "It is very discouraging to see lots at the Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park sitting idle, with lessees doing nothing with them or simply subleasing them to other businesses.

"It has also come to my attention that some lessees owe thousands of dollars in unpaid lease payments and are still allowed to operate. The sad part is that some of them are top government officials and prominent members of the community.

"Meanwhile, CTC, a company that my grandfather built from the ground up and which has grown into a household name in the construction and manufacturing industry, is not being given a fair opportunity to expand and grow."

LOCAL FAMILY-COMMUNITY ROOTS

Continental Transport Corporation (CTC) is one of American Samoa's larger locally owned construction and aggregate-supply companies. The company's roots go back to 1968, when the late Nu'utele Tiamo Togia'i started a small retail store and operated a single four-wheel bus.

After returning to American Samoa in 1970, his son, Fa'asefulu Togia'i, and wife, Elisapeta Togia'i, expanded the business, developing agricultural operations and growing the transportation side of the company. Over time, the business grew into a fleet of about 35 buses, becoming a major transportation provider on the eastern side of Tutuila. It was during this period that the company became known as Continental Transport Corporation (CTC).

In the mid-1990s, the family sold the bus transportation operation and shifted the company's focus to heavy construction. Starting with a dump truck, excavator, and backhoe, CTC expanded into earthmoving, infrastructure construction, aggregate production, equipment rentals, concrete production, and related services.

At present, CTC's operations extend well beyond general construction work. The company specializes in the production, retail sale, hauling, and storage of cinders, sand, rock aggregates, and other construction materials that are essential to infrastructure and development projects throughout the territory. It also provides laboratory testing services for construction materials, rents heavy equipment, performs truck and machinery maintenance and repairs, and manufactures concrete products used in both public and private construction projects.

Togia'i said the most suitable location for CTC's proposed brick and tri-bar manufacturing operation would be the stretch of industrial lots across from Veterans Memorial Stadium along Airport Road. The area is already home to similar heavy industrial activities, including a quarry operated by local contractor Paramount Builders. Just one lot away, McConnell Dowell, a construction and engineering company founded in New Zealand, operates a stone-crushing quarry and related facilities. The company has maintained a longstanding presence in American Samoa and has been involved in numerous public infrastructure projects throughout the Territory.

According to Togia'i, the lot situated between Paramount Builders and McConnell Dowell has remained vacant and undeveloped for years. He said he inquired about the possibility of leasing the property, only to discover that the lease is registered under the surname of a high-ranking government official.

"I don't know if the official himself is the lessee or if it's a relative," Togia'i said. "What I do know is that the lot has been sitting there unused for years while companies that actually need the land to create jobs and produce local products can't get access to it."

The lots along this section of Airport Road fall under the jurisdiction of the Department of Port Administration (DPA). They are also located within the broader area targeted for future development under the airport modernization component of the Vision 2030 initiative being advanced by DPA Director Barney Sene. Vision 2030 envisions a series of long-term improvements to airport infrastructure and surrounding properties, including commercial development opportunities, terminal upgrades, cargo-handling facilities, and other projects intended to support economic growth and modernize transportation infrastructure.

Togia'i acknowledged the importance of long-term development planning but questioned why strategically located industrial lots continue to sit idle while local companies seeking to expand their operations struggle to secure suitable sites.

"If the goal is economic development, then local businesses that have invested in American Samoa for generations should be part of that vision," he said. "We're ready to build, ready to hire, and ready to produce locally. All we're asking for is a fair opportunity."

By
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com
_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ For more than three decades, Continental Transport Corporation (CTC) has been a familiar name in American Samoa's construction industry, supplying building materials and providing services that support both government and private-sector projects. Today, however, the company finds itself at a crossroads.
After being denied permission twice by the American Samoa Zoning Board to relocate its retail and production operations, CTC owner Tony Togia'i says he is running out of options.
Frustrated by the repeated setbacks, Togia'i is now faced with the challenge of finding a suitable location where his company can resume full operations, continue serving customers, and generate enough revenue to pay employees, meet financial obligations, and keep the business afloat.
The CTC owner complained that their predicament is especially frustrating given his company's long service to the territory's development and infrastructure needs since the mid-1990s.
For more than a decade, CTC operated from its production and retail headquarters in Fogagogo near Maliu Mai Beach Resort, where it supplied construction materials and provided a range of services to contractors, homeowners, and government agencies. That chapter came to an end in 2025 when the company's lease expired and was not renewed.
Following the loss of its Fogagogo facility, Togia'i sought alternative locations that could accommodate CTC's extensive operations. Among the options pursued was space at the government-owned Senator Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park in Tafuna.

Seeking other options, Togia'i turned to Uili Leauanae, Deputy Director of the Department of Commerce (DOC). He said Leauanae informed him that there were no available lots within the Industrial Park that could accommodate the company's needs, leaving CTC with limited alternatives for relocating its operations.
Leauanae subsequently advised him that three vacant one-acre government lots were available for lease in the Vailoa-Leone area commonly known as the "Airstrip," and suggested that the company pursue the necessary approvals to secure one of the sites. According to Togia'i, Leauanae advised him to apply for a zoning variance and pursue a government lease for the property.
The area derives its nickname from the former Leone Airfield, a World War II-era military airstrip constructed by the U.S. Navy. The airfield once encompassed what are now several well-known landmarks, including Leone High School, Midkiff Elementary School, and the site of the former WVUV 648- AM radio station. Although the airfield was abandoned in early 1945 because of turbulent wind conditions and limited operational use, the area continues to be popularly known as the "Airstrip."

item.title: Roy Kim turns KSPO Dome into refuge for lovers on chilly night
item.description: For those familiar with K-pop, KSPO Dome in southern Seoul usually means an arena awash in synchronized lightsticks, with fans chanting between choreographed sets. On Friday, as singer-songwriter Roy Kim took the stage there for the first time in his career, the stands looked entirely different. Couples filled much of the arena, many huddled close against the first real chill of the season. In place of the usual lightsticks, a quieter kind of warmth rippled through the seating — the comfort of sitting beside someone you love on a cold night. The concert, "2026-27 Roy Kim Live Tour 'R:O:Y' in Seoul," runs through Sunday and marks a milestone for an artist who has built his career on ballads. After the originally scheduled weekend shows sold out, his agency, DEUL, added a Friday performance, which also sold out — a rare feat for a ballad singer at a venue many Korean musicians dream of headlining. Kim rose to fame by winning Mnet's audition program "Superstar K4" in 2012 and debuted the following year with "Bom Bom Bom," a breezy spring tune that became his signature. Writing and singi

item.title: Temple food offers more than just taste of Korea, Ven. Sunjae says
item.description: Korean temple food can offer more than a healthy, meat-free meal, Korean Buddhist temple food master Ven. Sunjae said Friday, inviting future travelers to discover the stories, seasonal rhythms and respect for nature behind the cuisine. Speaking at a forum held at Kyonggi University’s Seoul campus, Sunjae urged her audience to look beyond recipes and presentation to the relationships connecting food, people and the environment. More than 200 people, including professors, students and members of the public, attended the lecture, which was part of the university’s forum on the future of tourism. “When I went abroad, I never simply showed people food,” she said. “I always brought culture with it.” Her remarks offered an approach to culinary tourism through storytelling and participation rather than consumption. A meal, she explained, carries the history of its ingredients, the work of farmers and the customs of those who prepare and share it. item.title: Cold snap to bring subzero temperatures Saturday, with up to 8 cm of snow in North Jeolla Province
item.description: A cold snap is expected to bring subzero temperatures to most of the nation Saturday morning, with up to 8 centimeters of snow forecast for parts of North Jeolla Province, the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said Friday. Morning lows are expected to range from minus 8 to 3 degrees Celsius, with daytime highs of 1 to 11 degrees, below seasonal averages. Cold air moving south from the northwest will push temperatures below freezing across most regions. Morning lows in major cities are forecast at minus 5 degrees in Seoul and Incheon, minus 7 degrees in Chuncheon, minus 4 degrees in Daejeon, minus 3 degrees in Daegu, zero degrees in Gwangju and 1 degree in Busan. Daytime highs are expected to reach 2 degrees in Seoul, Incheon and Chuncheon, 4 degrees in Daejeon, 6 degrees in Daegu, 7 degrees in Gwangju and 8 degrees in Busan. Skies will be mostly clear nationwide, although South Chungcheong Province, North Jeolla Province, Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City and Jeju Island will be mostly cloudy. item.title: Lee approves appointment of new police chief
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung on Friday approved the appointment of Kim Jong-chul as new commissioner general of the Korean National Police Agency (KNPA), his office said. Lee's approval came after a parliamentary committee adopted a report on Kim's confirmation hearing with bipartisan support earlier this week. Kim will fill a post that has remained vacant for nearly two years since the former police chief was suspended from duty in connection with former President Yoon Suk Yeol's failed martial law bid in late 2024. The KNPA commissioner general can be appointed by the president without parliamentary consent following a confirmation hearing.

item.title: Siren-like college entrance exam alerts spark fears of emergency among some foreign nationals
item.description: Wyman Lau, a 38-year-old visitor from Hong Kong, was in a business meeting in Seoul on Wednesday when a loud, siren-like alert sounded on his phone. Lau, who is in Seoul on business from Wednesday through Saturday, checked the message but couldn’t read it because it was in Korean. It was one of two extreme emergency alerts the government sent to help detect cheating on the college entrance exam. “At first I even thought there was some major natural disaster such as a typhoon or earthquake,” Lau said Thursday. “After looking it up online, I found out it’s an anti-cheating measure for the college entrance exam. I thought it was quite interesting and a pretty creative approach.” He said Hong Kong has a similar alert system but rarely uses it, adding that “Hong Kongers live too comfortably. War wouldn't even cross their minds at first.” Lau seemed amused by the alerts, but some foreign residents and tourists found them disruptive because little information was available in languages other than Korean. War wouldn't even cross their minds at first.” Lau seemed amused by the alerts, but some foreign residents and tourists found them disruptive because little information was available in languages other than Korean. item.description: Relentless media and online scrutiny, along with the public's desire to see successful people fail, may have driven a man facing allegations of using artificial intelligence (AI) to cheat on exams to take his own life amid overwhelming social pressure, experts say. Their analysis followed the death by suicide of Lee Jin-woo — a Seoul National University dental student who drew widespread attention for being the first person to receive a perfect Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET) score. item.title: Seoul asks Uruguay to help resume Korea-Mercosur FTA talks
item.description: Seoul's First Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo asked Uruguay on Friday to play an "active" role in resuming negotiations on a free trade agreement between Korea and the South American trade bloc Mercosur in talks with his Uruguayan counterpart in Seoul, the foreign ministry said. Park made the call in the meeting with Uruguay's Deputy Foreign Minister Valeria Csukasi, noting that Uruguay serves as Mercosur's rotating chair in the second half of this year and coordinator for the trade negotiations with Korea, according to the ministry. Mercosur consists of Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia, along with several associate members. Korea and the bloc launched negotiations over a trade deal in 2018, but formal trade talks have stalled since 2021. item.title: Korean authority rejects request for full self-driving for China-made Teslas
item.description: Transportation regulators on Friday rejected Tesla’s request to allow its China-made vehicles to use full self-driving (FSD) technology in Korea, citing insufficient supporting documentation. According to the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, the Korea Transportation Safety Authority (KOTSA) informed Tesla Korea that its application for special approval of its FSD Supervised technology lacked sufficient documentation for a proper review and required further verification and additional materials. Tesla Korea submitted a five-page document to KOTSA via email on Oct. 22. The document consists of two pages of technical descriptions and three cover pages from a Dutch approval document. KOTSA said the technical descriptions contained only general information about FSD available on Tesla's website, while the company provided no detailed technical evidence or safety data needed for a regulatory review in Korea. The authority also said the submission included only the cover pages of the Dutch approval document, “without sufficient evidence, factual explanations or details to sup

item.title: Former trade policy chief reflects on $1 trillion exports milestone
item.description: Kim Jong-hoon, who led negotiations for the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA), described Korea's historic achievement of $1 trillion in exports as a remarkable accomplishment, but cautioned that a closer look reveals an economy heavily reliant on semiconductors. Speaking at the Korea Times headquarters in central Seoul on Tuesday, two days before the milestone was reached, Kim identified the country's growing dependence on semiconductors as a major downside of the achievement. "Put positively, semiconductors are driving exports. But from a more concerning perspective, we are overly dependent on a single sector," he said. "To strengthen our economic fundamentals, we need to build up areas where we remain vulnerable." According to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, cumulative exports from January to October this year reached $930 billion, an increase of approximately $350.9 billion from the same period last year. item.title: More Koreans want to marry, but financial hurdles remain
item.description: The share of Koreans who believe people should get married has reached its highest level since 2014, while the proportion who think married couples should have children has surpassed 70 percent for the first time. Although positive attitudes toward marriage and childbirth are recovering, financial circumstances remain the biggest obstacle discouraging people from tying the knot, a survey has found. The findings point to the need for policies that stabilize the living conditions of younger generations, particularly in housing and employment, to address the country's persistently low birthrate. According to the 2026 Social Survey released by the National Data Agency on Wednesday, 55 percent of people aged 13 and older said they believe people should get married. That was up 2.5 percentage points from two years earlier and the highest figure since 2014, when the proportion stood at 56.8 percent. Positive attitudes toward marriage had fallen to 48.1 percent in 2018 before recovering to 51.2 percent in 2020, 50 percent in 2022 and 52.5 percent in 2024. The latest figure marks a further increa

item.title: UN detention experts' visit to Korea postponed amid dispute over unannounced inspections
item.description: The foreign ministry said Friday it has postponed a planned visit by a U.N. working group on arbitrary detention following a disagreement over whether the experts should be allowed to make unannounced visits to prisons and other detention facilities. The government in January accepted a request from the U.N. Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) to visit Korea from Nov. 23 to Dec. 4 and held consultations with the entity and relevant domestic agencies from July through November, according to the ministry. During the consultations, the WGAD maintained that unannounced visits to prisons and other detention facilities were essential to its country visits, while authorities here concluded after reviewing relevant laws that they may not agree to such inspections. "Accordingly, the government decided to postpone the visit during the previously agreed period, taking into account the time needed for further consultations," the ministry said in a notice sent to reporters. "We are discussing ways to host the working group in a manner consistent with domestic laws and based on mutual respect

item.title: First lady Kim wants kimchi to go global like K-pop
item.description: First lady Kim Hea Kyung on Friday celebrated this year's Kimchi Day by visiting a kimchi fair and taking part in a kimchi-making event, expressing hope that the traditional Korean dish would go global like K-pop and K-culture. Attending a ceremony in southern Seoul marking the seventh Kimchi Day, which falls on Sunday this year, the first lady visited a kimchi fair showcasing the country's award-winning cabbage and radish kimchi varieties. She also visited a food competition featuring kimchi, where she sampled kimchi-based desserts, before taking part in a kimchi-making event. Kim noted that Korean culture, including kimchi, has gained widespread popularity around the world, from Europe and Africa to the Americas. "K-pop and K-culture are rapidly spreading across the world. That trend is important, and when it comes to kimchi and Korean food, people across the world will find it hard to give them up once they get used to them," Kim said. item.title: Ukraine was main topic at Trump-Putin meeting, Kremlin says
item.description: MOSCOW — The war in Ukraine dominated a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said on Thursday. The leaders also discussed two-way ties and their upcoming joint meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's southern city of Shenzhen, Ushakov added. Putin's mood after the meeting was "simply excellent", he said. The diplomatic gathering of the leaders of the world's largest nuclear powers is unlikely to yield major agreements, however, analysts say, given deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade. White House officials have said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of the Ukraine war during the three-way meeting, though Trump has suggested he could bring it up. He last met Putin in Alaska in 2025 for talks that failed to end the war.

item.title: Iran war costs surpass $48 bil. as lawmakers demand unreleased estimates on base damage
item.description: WASHINGTON — The costs of the Iran war have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13, but because that total does not include damage to U.S. bases attacked in the Middle East, lawmakers are pushing for the Pentagon to provide those figures. Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest overall cost estimate Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination to be Navy comptroller. The $48 billion figure includes the costs of military operations, as well as for replacing equipment and munitions. Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to U.S. installations, which Miller said he didn't have. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee’s chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible. An Associated Press analysis found that Iran attacked aircraft hangars, systems that detect incoming strikes, warehouses, troop housing and more, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage. item.title: Seoul stocks dip to 10-month low as AI worries spark Asia-wide tech sell-off
item.description: KOSPI plunged 5 percent Friday to a 10-month low, tracking a sharp sell-off in Asian technology stocks as concerns over returns on artificial intelligence (AI) investments deepened despite Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering (IPO). The benchmark index closed at 4,869.96, down 5.21 percent, marking its lowest finish since Jan. 20, when it closed at 4,885.75. The index opened 4.08 percent lower, and a sell-side sidecar was triggered at 11:54 a.m. Foreign and institutional investors sold a net 1.13 trillion won ($845.5 million) and 951.3 billion won in shares, respectively, on the main bourse, while retail investors bought a net 1.59 trillion won in shares. Elsewhere in Asia, Taiwan's benchmark index plunged 6.23 percent, while Japan's tumbled 4.74 percent. Anthropic's record-breaking IPO reaffirmed strong investor appetite for the AI sector. Still, remarks by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the possibility of issuing corporate bonds in the future rekindled concerns about the company's financing burden. item.title: Tents forcibly removed from site of ballot shortage protest after 169 days
item.description: Authorities began forcibly removing tents and other items Friday from a sit-in protest site at a Seoul park, ending a 169-day standoff triggered by unprecedented ballot shortages during the June 3 local elections. Officials of the Olympic Park in southern Seoul started clearing tents, chairs and other belongings at around 8 a.m. During the operation, clashes broke out between the officials and protesters, leaving one park official hospitalized with a head injury. Police said they arrested a female protester in her 70s in connection with the assault. The sit-in began on June 5 when protesters came to the park to block election officials from removing ballot boxes from the Olympic Park Handball Gymnasium, which served as a vote-counting facility. All ballot boxes were eventually retrieved on Oct. 29 by a team led by special counsel Lee Tae-han investigating irregularities linked to the June elections, but many protesters refused to leave. Park authorities initially asked the remaining protesters to voluntarily clear the site by Nov. 5, but later extended the deadline to Thursday. Sports aut

item.title: University of Seoul student wins agriculture category of World Bank Group AI hackathon
item.description: Moon Tae-yoon, a student in the Department of International Relations at the University of Seoul, has won first place in the agriculture track of the Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge hosted by the World Bank Group (WBG). Held from Oct. 3-4, the hackathon was designed to identify practical artificial intelligence (AI) solutions that can be deployed even in environments with limited internet access and electricity infrastructure. Competing as an individual, Moon presented “Dure,” an AI solution he independently conceptualized and developed. item.title: It takes only minutes for AI tool to ace all English, math CSAT questions
item.description: A paid Claude model answered every English reading and mathematics question correctly in a reporter-run test of the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), completing in minutes a set of problems that students spend many years preparing to solve. Even the free versions of artificial intelligence (AI) tools delivered impressive results. Perplexity answered 71 of the 74 questions correctly, making just one clear error and leaving two graphic-based questions unanswered. ChatGPT got every English reading question right, but fell short in mathematics, answering 32 of 46 questions correctly, with two wrong answers and 12 left unconfirmed. The models were given the 2027 academic-year university entrance exam papers, and their responses were checked against answer keys published by the state-run Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation. The test covered all 28 English reading questions, excluding the listening part, and 46 math questions across the common section and three electives. item.title: Lee's approval rating rises to 40 percent
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung's approval rating rose to 40 percent this week from the previous week, a Gallup Korea poll showed Friday. The survey, conducted from Tuesday through Thursday on 1,001 people aged 18 and older, showed that positive assessments of Lee's performance edged up 1 percentage point from the previous week, when the figure stood at 39 percent. Those who disapproved of Lee's handling of state affairs edged down to 49 percent, while 10 percent withheld their opinion. Lee's approval rating has fluctuated between the high 30s and low-to-mid 40s since reaching 44 percent in the second week of August. Among those who positively assessed Lee's performance, 24 percent cited diplomacy as the main reason, followed by economic and livelihood issues at 12 percent, communication at 9 percent, and policies for ordinary people and welfare at 7 percent. Economic and livelihood issues were cited by 18 percent of those who disapproved of Lee's performance, making them the most frequently cited reason. item.title: BTS becomes 1st non-Japanese artist to top 10 bln streams in Japan
item.description: K-pop supergroup BTS has racked up more than 10 billion streams in Japan, in the first such record for a non-Japanese artist, the group's agency said Friday. It also marks the fifth record for any musical act to accomplish in Japan, BigHit Music said, citing Billboard Japan. A total of 27 BTS songs have each amassed more than 100 million streams in the country, including "Dynamite" with 1 billion streams and "Butter" with 600 million streams. The group's fifth studio album, "Arirang," released in March, topped Billboard Japan's comprehensive albums chart in the first half, and also ranked No. 1 in terms of CD sales and streams. "This milestone demonstrates how different hit tracks have enjoyed popularity over a long time," BigHit said. On Thursday, BTS launched the Asian and Australian leg of its "Arirang" world tour in Taiwan's Kaohsiung, with 26 performances scheduled across nine cities.

item.title: Industry minister calls for new growth engine to go beyond $1 tril. in exports
item.description: Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said Friday that Korea needs to make further efforts to overcome lingering challenges, such as industrial polarization, and share the benefits of the recent artificial intelligence (AI) boom across the broader economy to sustain growth. Kim made the remarks during a meeting with executives of six major trade associations, including the Federation of Korean Industries and the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry, to mark the country reaching $1 trillion in annual exports. Korea's exports surpassed the $1 trillion mark as of Thursday, making it the fourth country in the world to achieve the feat, following the United States, Germany and China. The milestone was driven by strong demand for semiconductors stemming from global investments in AI infrastructure. While congratulating local businesses and exporters on the achievement, Kim pointed out that many challenges remain to be addressed. item.title: Lee Jae-keun takes helm at KB Financial Group, setting stage for generational shake-up
item.description: Lee Jae-keun’s appointment as new head of KB Financial Group was approved at an extraordinary general meeting on Friday, setting the stage for a broader generational transition at Korea's largest financial group. At the meeting held at KB Kookmin Bank headquarters in Yeouido, Seoul, Lee received 97.69 percent support from shareholders represented, equivalent to 76.14 percent of the group’s total outstanding shares. He is set to take office Saturday after board approval, succeeding outgoing Chairman Yang Jong-hee, for a three-year term running through November 2029. He is expected to lay out his management priorities and vision at an inauguration ceremony on Monday. item.title: Foreign game developers fill Korean firms' absence at G-Star game expo
item.description: Foreign game developers have filled the gap left by the absence of a number of major Korean game firms at G-Star 2026, the country's largest game expo in Busan, with Chinese firms expanding their presence. The G-Star 2026 kicked off its four-day run on Thursday, with 1,237 companies from 41 countries opening booths at BEXCO exhibition center in Haeundae District, Busan. The number of companies participating declined by 36 compared to last year’s edition. This year's G-Star raised concerns as four of Korea's five major game companies — Nexon, NC, Netmarble and Kakao Games — skipped the event, leaving Krafton as the only company setting up a booth among the five. Filling the gap left by their absence were foreign game developers. China's HoYoverse returned to G-Star for the first time in four years, setting up a large exhibition space to offer the first hands-on demonstrations in Korea of its upcoming titles Honkai: Nexus Anima and Petit Planet. The company also prepared various interactive programs using its existing games, including Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail and Zenless Zon

item.title: Anthropic's record IPO: Which Korean companies stand to gain?
item.description: Early investments by Korean tech companies in Anthropic have paid off handsomely following the artificial intelligence (AI) giant's record-breaking initial public offering (IPO), industry officials said Friday. SK Telecom, in particular, hit the jackpot. The company made an initial $100 million investment in Anthropic in 2023, followed by additional investments that brought its total commitment to around $200 million. After accounting for Anthropic's 10-for-1 stock split in September, SK Telecom holds approximately 38.6 million shares, valued at around $3.75 billion based on Anthropic's closing share price on Thursday, its first day of trading. SK Telecom is weighing a sale of its Anthropic stake. During its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 4, the company said it would consider its long-term investment plans, including AI data centers, funding needs and financial conditions, when deciding how to use proceeds from a potential sale. item.title: Founder's acquittal expected to accelerate Kakao's restructuring
item.description: A high court ruling acquitting Kakao founder and Future Initiative Center head Kim Beom-su of charges related to alleged stock price manipulation during Kakao's 2023 takeover battle for SM Entertainment is expected to ease uncertainties surrounding the platform company's corporate restructuring efforts. The Seoul High Court on Friday upheld a lower court ruling clearing Kim of allegations that he manipulated SM Entertainment's stock price, saying prosecutors failed to prove that he intended to manipulate the share price through artificial means. "Although all transactions in the stock market can affect market prices, punishing all buying activities on that basis alone could lead to an unlimited expansion of the scope of criminal liability," the court said. Former Kakao Chief Investment Officer Bae Jae-hyun, former Kakao CEO Hong Eun-taek and other executives were also cleared of stock manipulation charges. item.title: Korea cracks down on illegal online sales of GLP-1 obesity drugs
item.description: The Ministry of Food and Drug Safety said Thursday it is launching a crackdown on illegal online sales, brokering and advertising of GLP-1 obesity drugs amid increasing demand. The crackdown covers sales through direct purchases from overseas sellers and secondhand trading. The ministry warned that individuals who bring in such drugs from abroad for personal treatment violate the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act if they resell them or give them to others. It plans to take stern action against violators, including requesting investigations and filing criminal complaints. Since Nov. 12, the government has allowed up to a three-month supply of obesity drugs prescribed overseas to be carried into the country. The change has raised concerns that more buyers would purchase cheaper drugs such as Mounjaro and Wegovy there to resell at home. Exact prices may vary, but a four-week supply of Mounjaro at its lowest dose costs about 300,000 won ($224) in Korea, roughly three times what some medical institutions in Japan charge.
