item.title: President calls for sweeping overhaul of national testing system
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung called for a swift overhaul of the national testing system, Friday, a day after the national college entrance exam, amid concerns raised by reports of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cheating on other national tests. “We need to revamp the national testing system quickly and completely, from A to Z, to keep up with changing conditions,” Lee said during a meeting with senior presidential aides at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul. “I ask you to take bold measures, backed by close coordination, to ensure fairness in the College Scholastic Ability Test as well as in all other exams or assessments conducted across the public and private sectors.” The president instructed officials to review how other countries have responded, examine relevant technology trends and consider proposals from experts and input from the public. “I ask you to draw up a comprehensive plan that leaves no gaps as quickly as possible,” he said. item.title: SK hynix to convert Kioxia-related bonds into shares
item.description: Korean chip giant SK hynix Inc. said Friday it will convert convertible bonds (CBs) linked to its investment in Kioxia Corp., a Japanese NAND flash memory maker, into shares, becoming the Japanese company's largest indirect shareholder. In a regulatory filing, SK hynix said it will convert 129 billion yen ($810.3 million) worth of CBs issued by SPC2 (BCPE Pangea Cayman2 Ltd.), a special-purpose company, into 129,000 common shares. The company also plans to acquire an additional 1,001 common shares in SPC2 from U.S. private equity firm Bain Capital for 100 million yen. Upon completion of the transactions, SK hynix will indirectly hold a 14.1 percent stake in Kioxia through SPC2, making it the Japanese company's largest indirect shareholder. Toshiba held a 10.46 percent stake as of early November, making it the second-largest shareholder. SK hynix said the CB conversion is a follow-up measure to reorganize its investment structure following the liquidation of its equity fund. item.title: K-pop girl group aespa joins Disney holiday special alongside global music stars
item.description: Korean girl group aespa will join Kelly Clarkson and Alanis Morissette on Disney’s annual holiday television special later this month, marking another high-profile U.S. broadcast appearance for the quartet. The four-member group will appear on "The Wonderful World of Disney: Holiday Spectacular," scheduled to air Nov. 30 on ABC in the United States, performing the English-language songs "Santa Baby" and "KISS N TELL" against the backdrop of the Walt Disney World Resort in Orlando, Florida, SM Entertainment said. The special will be hosted by Derek Hough, an Emmy-winning choreographer and performer, with narration by Quinta Brunson, an actress and producer who has won Golden Globe and Emmy awards. Other performers scheduled to appear include Madison Beer and Anthony Ramos, placing aespa alongside established international artists in the holiday broadcast. The appearance adds another high-profile international engagement for the group, which has continued to expand its touring activities across several continents. item.title: ATEEZ surpasses 2 mil. 1st-week album sales in career milestone
item.description: K-pop group ATEEZ topped 2 million first-week sales with its latest release, marking a career first for the eight-member act. The group’s 15th EP, “Golden Hour: Part. 6,” which came out Nov. 13, sold 2,055,545 copies in its first week, according to Hanteo Chart, a Korean service that tracks album sales in real time. In the K-pop industry, first-week sales are a closely watched measure of how big a group’s fan base is. That beats the roughly 1.88 million first-week copies of its previous EP, “Golden Hour: Part. 5,” and is the group’s best result so far, the group’s agency KQ Entertainment said. Before the album came out, the group released the song “Drip” in advance. It debuted at No. 190 on the Billboard Global 200 chart dated Nov. 7. That chart ranks songs by streaming and sales in more than 200 countries and territories. It was the first time an ATEEZ song had entered the chart in its first week of release. item.title: SANTOS BRAVOS, &TEAM release 2nd collaboration 'ORIGAMI'
item.description: SANTOS BRAVOS, a Latin pop boy band from HYBE, released “ORIGAMI,” its second collaboration with Japanese boy group &TEAM, at midnight Friday. The song sets the two groups’ voices over Latin rhythms. It opens with gentle guitar before rhythmic percussion builds in, and the lyrics switch among Spanish, English and Japanese. The groups’ first collaboration, “KAWASAKI (&TEAM Remix),” released in February, was built on hard-hitting beats and high energy. HYBE says “ORIGAMI” is more mature and emotional in tone. The song takes its theme from origami, the traditional Japanese art of folding paper into shapes. Just as each fold gives the paper a new form, the lyrics describe growing through experiences and the people one meets along the way. The creases left behind stand for lessons learned and relationships formed. The song also promises to move forward without losing one’s roots, and it thanks the family, friends and communities that offered support along the way. item.title: No signs of foul play found in autopsy of LEET top scorer
item.description: Officials have not found any signs of foul play from the autopsy of the top scorer on this year's law school entrance exam, who was suspected of cheating, sources said Friday, one day after the 32-year-old failed to show up for a live broadcast in which he promised to prove his scholastic abilities. Lee Jin-woo, a student at Seoul National University School of Dentistry, was found dead at a Seoul motel Thursday after facing intense public scrutiny over suspicions he cheated on the test. The National Forensic Service conducted an autopsy on Lee's body but so far has found no evidence of foul play, according to the sources. Lee, who scored full marks on the Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET), faced suspicions he cheated on the test by using artificial intelligence (AI). He was supposed to appear on a YouTube channel early Thursday to prove his academic abilities by taking a Korean language test from this year's college entrance exam but never showed up, prompting a police search. item.title: Universities tighten rules to curb AI cheating on weekend essay exams
item.description: Universities are tightening security ahead of this weekend’s college entrance essay exams, with some checking eyeglasses, restricting personal writing tools and issuing disposable aprons to prevent cheating with artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled devices. A total of 14 schools, including Korea University, Sogang University, Sungkyunkwan University and Kyung Hee University, will hold essay exams Saturday and Sunday, the first weekend after Thursday’s national College Scholastic Ability Test. In all, 36 universities are scheduled to hold essay exams after the national test. The Ministry of Education held an online meeting Friday morning with admissions officials from 56 universities to share preparations and discuss how to prevent candidates from using smart devices to cheat on upcoming exams. The measures follow incidents last month at Yonsei University and the University of Seoul, where applicants were caught using AI-enabled smart glasses during essay exams. item.title: S. Korea returns to No. 1 in UN e-government survey after 12 years
item.description: South Korea has reclaimed the world's top spot in a United Nations survey of e-government development for the first time in 12 years, the interior ministry said Friday. In the U.N. E-Government Survey 2026, South Korea ranked first among 194 countries in the E-Government Development Index (EGDI), scoring 0.9794, the ministry said. Denmark came in second with 0.9777, followed by Singapore with 0.9722, Saudi Arabia 0.9721 and the United Arab Emirates 0.9711. The United States placed 13th with a score of 0.9440, while Japan came in 29th with 0.8968 and China 41st with 0.8743. North Korea ranked 190th, with a score of 0.2166, according to the ministry. Since 2002, the U.N. has conducted a biennial assessment of e-government development across its 193 member states. This year, Palestine was also included in the evaluation. The EGDI measures the level of e-government development based on three components: the Online Service Index (OSI), the Telecommunication Infrastructure Index (TII) and the Human Capital Index (HCI). item.title: Late actor likely to be stripped of state honor over alleged link to N. Korea in Korean War
item.description: A Korea-born Chinese actor renowned for starring in a number of movies that encouraged anti-Japanese sentiments in the 1930s will likely be stripped of his South Korean state medal for his activities linked to North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War, informed sources said Friday. Kim Duk-rin, who is better known as Jin Yan in China, was posthumously awarded South Korea's Aejok Order of Merit for National Foundation on the Aug. 15 Liberation Day, a national holiday celebrating Korea's liberation from the 1910-45 Japanese colonial rule. The late actor came under scrutiny soon after as a media report claimed that he was part of a Chinese delegation dispatched to North Korea in 1952 to help boost the morale of Chinese and North Korean troops fighting against South Korean and U.N. forces in the Korean War. An evaluation committee held a meeting last Friday to review his case and decided in favor of a motion to strip Kim of his state medal, the sources familiar with the matter told Yonhap News Agency. item.title: New mortgage loans per borrower rise slightly in Q3
item.description: New mortgage loans per borrower edged up in the third quarter from three months earlier on steady demand in Seoul and its surrounding areas, central bank data showed Friday. Fresh mortgage lending per borrower averaged 214.51 million won ($160,500) during the July-September period, up 6.22 million won from three months earlier, according to data from the Bank of Korea (BOK). The third-quarter increase followed a record on-quarter 21.1 million-won drop in the previous three-month period. New household lending per borrower, which includes mortgage loans, fell 3.86 million won to 30.28 million won over the cited period, marking the lowest since the fourth quarter of 2022. By region, fresh mortgage lending in the greater Seoul area rose by 13.23 million won per borrower in the third quarter, while that in the Gangwon region increased by 54.81 million won. By age group, new mortgage loans taken out by borrowers in their 30s and 40s rose by 7.76 million won and 6.47 million won, respectively. Borrowers in their 20s and 50s took out 7.46 million won and 2.37 million won less in new mortgage loans

item.title: Navy chief to visit Japan, Tahiti for talks on maritime cooperation
item.description: Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Kim Kyung-ryul will visit Japan and Tahiti next week for high-level talks with his counterparts on boosting maritime cooperation and military exchanges, the Navy said Friday. Kim will make a two-day trip to Japan starting Sunday, during which he plans to meet with Adm. Akira Saito, chief of staff of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF), and discuss ways to strengthen maritime security cooperation, including high-level and unit-level exchanges, the Navy said. While in Japan, Kim is also scheduled to visit the JMSDF's Yokosuka District to meet with its commandant, Vice Adm. Koji Yagi, it said. Kim will then travel to Tahiti, the island of French Polynesia, to attend a regional naval conference, where naval chiefs and commanders from around 30 countries will gather to discuss regional maritime security cooperation. Kim Kyung-ryul will visit Japan and Tahiti next week for high-level talks with his counterparts on boosting maritime cooperation and military exchanges, the Navy said Friday. Kim will make a two-day trip to Japan starting Sunday, during which he plans to meet with Adm. Akira Saito, chief of staff of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF), and discuss ways to strengthen maritime security cooperation, including high-level and unit-level exchanges, the Navy said. While in Japan, Kim is also scheduled to visit the JMSDF's Yokosuka District to meet with its commandant, Vice Adm. Koji Yagi, it said. Kim will then travel to Tahiti, the island of French Polynesia, to attend a regional naval conference, where naval chiefs and commanders from around 30 countries will gather to discuss regional maritime security cooperation. item.title: KRX activates sell-side sidecar for KOSPI on sharp fall
item.description: South Korea's bourse operator on Friday activated a sell-side sidecar for the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) as the stock index plunged. Program trading for the KOSPI-listed shares was suspended for five minutes from 11:54 a.m., according to the Korea Exchange (KRX). The KOSPI surrendered 233.2 points, or 4.54 percent, to 4,904.69 as of 11:55 a.m. The index came under downward pressure as Anthropic's solid market debut failed to ease concerns over whether heavy investment in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure will generate returns. A sell-side sidecar is triggered when the KOSPI 200 Futures Index falls 5 percent or more for at least one minute.

item.title: Foreign firms in Korea raise wages 3.9%, expect slower growth in 2027
item.description: Foreign-invested companies in Korea increased wages by an average of 3.9 percent this year, but expect raises to ease in 2027, according to a new industry survey that offers a detailed look at compensation trends across multinational businesses operating in the country. The Korea Foreign Enterprise Association (KOFA) said in November that its eighth annual white paper found companies expect average wage increases of 3.6 percent in 2027, down 0.3 percentage points from this year's figure. The findings are based on a compensation survey of 96 foreign-invested companies conducted by KOFA HR Lab, the research arm of the association's human resources organization, between June 1 and Nov. 13. The survey found that average bonuses amounted to 13.8 percent of annual salaries, while sales incentives averaged 23.6 percent. More than half of participating companies, or 56.3 percent, differentiated pay according to job responsibilities, while 37.5 percent operated an inclusive wage system. item.title: Over 110 caught with illegal electronic devices during CSAT: ministry
item.description: A total of 111 cases of alleged cheating involving electronic devices took place during the annual national college entrance exam this week, the education ministry said Friday, sharply raising the final tally from the 98 announced the previous day. Of the total, 54 cases were identified after the government sent disaster alerts to mobile phones nationwide as part of strengthened anti-cheating measures for the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) on Thursday, according to the ministry. Authorities also found 52 cases through other methods, such as by detecting Wi-Fi signals, while five were caught red-handed using smart devices. The government stepped up measures to root out cheating this year following widespread public outrage over the recent confession of the top scorer of this year's tax accountant exam that he had cheated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital devices. item.title: Italian chef says Korean food deserves its own story abroad
item.description: Italian chef Daniele Lippi, head chef of the two-Michelin-star Acquolina restaurant in Rome, returned to Korea this week to lead a masterclass reinterpreting classic Italian dishes as part of the 2026 Week of Italian Cuisine in the World. The Thursday masterclass was held ahead of a gala dinner hosted jointly by the Italian Embassy in Seoul and the Italian Chamber of Commerce in Korea. It is Lippi’s second visit to Korea. His first, a 10-day trip, included an appearance on the television program “Welcome, First Time in Korea?” "I liked Korea so much that I didn't hesitate for even a second," Lippi told The Korea Times in an interview. During the masterclass, Lippi presented potato gnocchi and a creative take on spaghetti alla marinara. Instead of using tomatoes as the base, he used a rosehip infusion to recreate the familiar flavor of the classic Italian dish. Such experimentation, Lippi said, is not about abandoning tradition but using it as a foundation for creativity. "I think it is extremely important to use memories of traditional flavors as a foundation for creativity," he said

item.title: Aspiring accountants face tougher odds as AI reshapes hiring, shakes confidence in CPA exam
item.description: “It feels deeply unfair that the people who played by the rules and worked hard are the ones paying the price. If the top scorer hadn’t admitted to cheating, we might have carried on without ever realizing that we had been denied a fair shot,” said one candidate who has spent at least three years preparing for Korea’s certified public accountant (CPA) exam and missed the passing score by less than a point. His comments followed revelations that the top scorer in this year’s certified tax accountant exam admitted to using generative artificial intelligence (AI) and electronic devices to cheat, earning near-perfect marks. The candidate also confessed to using the same methods during the CPA exam, although he failed to pass. “Given what has come to light, it seems almost naive to assume that nobody has cheated their way through the CPA exam in the past two or three years,” he added. “I’m stunned. It really makes you question everything.” The scandal has unsettled not only those still studying for the exams but also people who have already passed. Many are entering a pro

item.title: POSCO 1% Foundation equips wounded vets with high-tech mobility gear
item.description: The POSCO 1% Foundation, a charity funded by POSCO Group employees, gave customized high-tech assistive devices to 26 wounded veterans and uniformed workers Thursday, the foundation said. At a ceremony at the Veterans Health Service Medical Center in Seoul, the foundation gave devices to eight people recognized for their service to the nation and to 18 active-duty soldiers and firefighters. It also provided advanced rehabilitation equipment to two newly designated affiliated veterans hospitals in Gangwon Province and on Jeju Island. The public hospitals give veterans in regions without a dedicated veterans hospital a comparable level of care closer to home. The foundation launched the program in 2020 with the Ministry of Patriots and Veterans Affairs. It provides equipment such as robotic prosthetic arms and legs, artificial intelligence-powered hearing aids and advanced wheelchairs to help veterans injured in service live independently. item.title: US maritime agency delegation tours HD Hyundai Heavy's Ulsan shipyard
item.description: A delegation led by Mark D. Johnson, deputy administrator of the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD), visited HD Hyundai Heavy Industries’ shipyard in Ulsan to view its shipbuilding technology and discuss shipbuilding cooperation between Korea and the U.S., HD Hyundai said Friday. MARAD is an agency under the U.S. Department of Transportation. It moves military supplies during national emergencies and supports improvements to port infrastructure. The visit comes as Washington pursues what it calls the Bridge Strategy, which aims to rebuild the U.S. shipbuilding industry by using allies’ technology and production capacity while expanding shipbuilding capacity in the U.S. Under a presidential memorandum issued in August, foreign shipbuilders that meet certain conditions, such as owning a shipyard in the U.S., can build up to the first two ships of a program overseas. item.title: Sungkyunkwan University professor explores limits of AI language models in new book
item.description: Lee Han-jung, a professor in the Department of English Language and Literature at Sungkyunkwan University, is set to publish an English-language book titled “Polysemy in Semantics with Contextualized Language Models” next month, the university said. The book will be published by De Gruyter Brill, a renowned international academic publisher. It presents a new artificial intelligence (AI)-based methodology for studying linguistic meaning. It is the latest addition to “Language and Computers,” an academic book series launched in 1988 that publishes outstanding works in digital linguistics selected through a rigorous peer-review process. The book is particularly significant in that it bridges lexical semantics, traditionally rooted in the humanities, with computational models powered by advanced AI technologies. item.title: KT, LG Electronics transmit files using quantum particles, aiming for unhackable networks
item.description: In a step toward virtually unhackable networks, KT and LG Electronics have transmitted and restored text and image data by encoding information directly onto quantum particles rather than conventional digital signals, the telecom operator said Friday. The technology is called quantum secure direct communication (QSDC). It differs from quantum key distribution (QKD), the more established form of quantum cryptography. QKD uses quantum signals only to share the keys that encrypt a message. QSDC puts the message itself into quantum states, which are fragile physical properties of particles such as photons. Those states are disturbed if anyone tries to intercept them. KT encoded 1,024 bits of image data into quantum signals, sent them and restored the image at the receiving end. It also used the same system to transmit text data. The two companies have been working together since signing an agreement in 2025 to develop next-generation quantum internet technology. item.title: Sogang University team secures Samsung funding for advanced materials research
item.description: A research project led by professors at Sogang University has been selected for the Samsung Science & Technology Foundation’s research support program, a major initiative aimed at fostering innovative scientific breakthroughs. Kim Hyeong-jun, a professor in the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, will conduct the research in collaboration with Sung Bong-june, a professor in the Department of Chemistry, the university said. Titled “Achieving Ceramic-Level Ultra-High Dielectric Permittivity in Flexible Elastomers Through Orientational Polarization of Ionic Dipoles,” the study aims to develop polymer materials that combine exceptionally high dielectric permittivity with mechanical flexibility, potentially paving the way for next-generation flexible electronic devices. Launched by Samsung Group in 2013, the foundation’s program supports challenging research in basic science, materials technology and information and communications technology convergence. item.title: Korean tourism startups court North American market at US industry showcase
item.description: The Korea Tourism Organization (KTO) brought five Korean tourism startups to a major U.S. travel industry conference this week to help them break into the North American market, the state-run agency said Friday. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the KTO took part in Phocuswright Conference 2026, held Tuesday through Thursday in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Organized by U.S. travel market research firm Phocuswright, the annual event brings together industry leaders to examine changes in travel technology, mobility and artificial intelligence (AI). The five firms were recruited from companies selected for KTO support programs, including one that helps tourism startups expand overseas, and had been judged ready to enter foreign markets. item.title: Flying squirrels find refuge in wooden boxes in charred Korean forest
item.description: More than a year after a massive wildfire tore through the mountains of southeastern Korea, signs of recovery are emerging in the treetops, where an endangered species of nocturnal flying squirrel has begun breeding inside handcrafted wooden shelters. Biologists with the National Institute of Ecology announced Friday that up to six Siberian flying squirrels, classified as a Class II endangered species in Korea, were observed living and reproducing between July and October inside artificial nest boxes installed in Yeongyang County, North Gyeongsang Province. The shelters were hung in October 2025 around Janggumegi Wetland, an abandoned terraced rice paddy converted into a mountain wetland that spans roughly 11 acres. Designated as a national wetland protection area in September 2024, the site harbors 458 wildlife species, including six endangered animals such as the yellow-throated marten, the leopard cat and the fairy pitta. In March 2025, a sweeping wildfire devastated the surrounding woodland, depriving forest-dwelling creatures of critical shelter. Ecological restoration specialists

item.title: S. Korean firm plans $150 mil. lifeline for Eric Trump-backed robot maker
item.description: NEW YORK — South Korean conglomerate Base Group is preparing to invest $150 million in a struggling military-robot maker backed by US President Donald Trump's son Eric, internal company emails show, deepening the firm’s ties to the Trump family that have already drawn congressional scrutiny. Foundation Future Industries, which makes gun-carrying “Terminator”-style robot soldiers and employs Eric Trump as chief strategy adviser, stopped paying employees in recent weeks and is pinning its future on Base Group’s funding, according to CEO Sankaet Pathak's emails to employees seen by Reuters. “My read, given where Base is, this is a timing issue, not an existential one for the company,” Pathak wrote in a November 8 email, referring to the payroll issues. A Base Group spokesperson confirmed the company was considering an investment in Foundation, "recognizing the long-term value and growth potential of humanoid robotics,” but did not respond to further questions. item.title: Seoul turns iconic landmarks into free 3D backdrops for webtoon creators
item.description: Seoul is turning some of its most recognizable landmarks into ready-made digital backdrops, giving webtoon and animation creators around the world free access to 3D versions of the city's streets, shopping districts and Han River waterfront. The Seoul Metropolitan Government said Friday it will distribute 13 digital assets featuring locations across the capital, including Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP), Yeouido Park and Banpo Hangang Park, through ACON, a global digital asset platform. The collection includes five outdoor locations and eight indoor settings, expanding on an initial plan announced in March to produce 3D backgrounds of about two major Seoul landmarks. The outdoor settings cover two areas around Dongdaemun — DDP and its fashion district, as well as Heunginji Gate and Cheonggye Stream — and three along the Han River, including Yeouido Park and Yeouidaero, Yeouido Hangang Park and Banpo Bridge and Some Sevit. item.description: Bone AI, a Korean defense technology company, is joining a government-backed project to develop domestically made semiconductor technology for disaster detection, with plans to test an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered sensor system on its wildfire-monitoring drones. The company said Friday it will participate in a 10.75 billion won ($7.9 million) research and development project led by Daegu University under the Ministry of Science and ICT's 2026 Science and Technology Innovation Support Program. The project, scheduled to run through 2030, brings together 10 industry, academic and research institutions, including Bone AI subsidiary Dmakers. At its core is the development of a multisensory module that combines data from smoke, flame and gas sensors to identify potential hazards at industrial sites and other locations. The system is designed to reduce reliance on foreign sensors and AI chips by using domestically developed semiconductor technology. item.description: Washington — US President Donald Trump has said he still considers Elon Musk a friend, despite the tech billionaire attempting to distance himself from Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement. Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Musk told The New York Times on Wednesday that he was "not MAGA." Speaking to NBC News on Thursday, Trump said Elon was "a friend of mine." item.title: Man referred to prosecution on suspicion of killing teen victim of son's alleged sex crime
item.description: Police on Friday referred a man to the prosecution on suspicion of killing a teenage girl alleged to have been sexually assaulted by his son, officials said. The 59-year-old was referred to the Seoul Northern District Prosecutors Office, according to the Seoul Seongbuk Police Station. During questioning, the suspect said he killed the teenager on impulse out of anger while asking her to submit a written statement saying she did not wish for his son to be punished, the police said. Police placed the man under emergency arrest last week after finding the female victim dead at a house listed on Airbnb in Seoul's northeastern Seongbuk Ward. He was reportedly drunk at the time of his arrest. The victim's parents had filed a complaint in March against the murder suspect's son, accusing him of having sexual relations with their daughter in January. The son is currently in detention for another crime.

item.title: BIGBANG drops new single 'GiiiRIP'
item.description: Iconic K-pop group BIGBANG released its new single "GiiiRIP" on Friday, the act's agency said, in another event marking its 20th anniversary this year. Released at 2 p.m., the new song conveys the group's firm determination to continue expanding its musical prowess and rewrite its history, according to YG Entertainment. When spoken, "GiiiRIP" sounds like the Korean word "girip," which means to stand up. BIGBANG member G-Dragon took part in writing and composing the song, while member Taeyang also took part in penning the lyrics, the agency said. In August, BIGBANG released "BiiiG," the group's first new song in four years and four months since "Still Life" was released in April 2022. The group is currently on its "XX: Cosmos" world tour and is set to perform at the MAMA Awards, one of K-pop's biggest year-end music events, in Osaka this weekend.

item.title: Hyundai Motor unveils new Elantra, Genesis G80 Hybrid at LA Auto Show
item.description: Hyundai Motor said Friday it has unveiled its eighth-generation Avante compact sedan, known as the Elantra in North America, and the Genesis G80 Hybrid at the Los Angeles Auto Show. The Korean automaker showcased the all-new 2027 Elantra and 2028 Elantra Hybrid during a media preview of the auto show at the Los Angeles Convention Center in California. The all-new Elantra will be available with two powertrain options: a 2.0-liter gasoline engine and a 1.6-liter hybrid powertrain. Genesis, Hyundai Motor's luxury brand, also unveiled the G80 Hybrid with enhanced power output and fuel efficiency. The G80 Hybrid combines a 2.5-liter turbocharged gasoline engine with a dual-motor hybrid system, offering a driving range of approximately 1,029 kilometers on a single tank of fuel. The model also features a liquid-cooled battery system for improved thermal efficiency and higher discharge power compared with air-cooled systems.

item.title: Seoul subway union launches 'work-to-rule' campaign over hiring, wage dispute
item.description: Unionized workers at Seoul Metro launched a "work-to-rule" campaign Friday as they remain locked in a dispute with management over hiring and wages. Under the collective action that began at 6 a.m., participants will fully adhere to safety regulations, such as maintaining train speeds regardless of subway schedules, in a move expected to slow down operations. The union plans to continue the collective action and launch an indefinite strike next Wednesday unless the management responds to its demands for an additional hiring of 1,313 personnel and a wage increase of 3.5 percent. It has also called for the management to scrap a plan to cut 2,212 jobs. Unionized workers of Korea Railroad Corp. (KORAIL) have also warned of launching an indefinite general strike on Dec. 10, demanding the hiring of more safety-related personnel.

item.title: Seoul shares extend losses late Friday morning on tech slump
item.description: Seoul shares extended losses late Friday morning as investors remain concerned over whether heavy investment in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure will generate returns. After opening 4.08 percent lower, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell 218.03 points, or 4.24 percent, to 4,919.86 as of 11:20 a.m. Overnight, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 2.19 percent, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 2.25 percent. Institutions and foreigners sold a net 443.61 billion won ($331 million) and 760.54 billion won worth of stocks, respectively. Individuals bought a net 1.01 trillion won. Investors are awaiting further evidence that the AI boom will ultimately generate sustainable returns large enough to justify the industry's massive borrowings. Anthropic shares soared 17 percent above their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83 to close at $97.17 on Thursday (U.S. time) on Wall Street. item.title: Unification minister, top US envoy reaffirm alliance as key to peace in 1st talks
item.description: Unification Minister Chung Dong-young met U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel on Friday to discuss the allies' policies on North Korea and Seoul's effort to bring lasting peace on the Korean Peninsula, the ministry said. It was Chung's first official meeting with Steel, who arrived here in late July as Washington's top envoy to Seoul. The ministry had confirmed last month that the talks were being arranged. At Chung's office at the government complex in Seoul, the two discussed the situation on the Korean Peninsula and the allies' North Korea policies, the ministry said in a statement. Chung called a firm South Korea-U.S. alliance the foundation of peace and prosperity on the peninsula, and said dialogue with Pyongyang must resume, both between Washington and Pyongyang, and between the two Koreas. He explained Seoul's effort to keep border tensions from flaring into accidental clashes and to build peaceful coexistence, and asked for Washington's support. item.title: N. Korea, Laos vow deeper cooperation in Pyongyang meeting
item.description: Officials from North Korea and Laos have met in Pyongyang to discuss measures to expand cooperation in the economy, trade, and science and technology sectors, Pyongyang's state media reported Friday. The fourth session of the joint committee on economic, trade, scientific and technological cooperation was held at the Pyongyang Assembly Hall on Thursday, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said. Yun Jong-ho, the North's external economic relations minister, led the country's delegation, while Malaithong Kommasith, Laos' industry and commerce minister, headed that of Laos. The two sides "discussed in detail the practical items of bilateral cooperation" in those areas and signed a protocol at the end of the session, the report said. North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song met Kommasith and other Lao officials for talks that the KCNA said were held "in a friendly atmosphere." A separate party-level exchange took place the same day. item.title: Trump says no rush on Iran decision, looks to next year
item.description: WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump on Thursday appeared to push a decision on renewed major strikes against Iran into next year, extending a timeline that he had previously suggested could come to a head after this month's US midterm elections. Asked in an interview with Reuters about the possibility of new strikes, Trump said: “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.” “We’ve got time," added Trump, speaking from his plane as he returned to Washington from his trip to China. In recent weeks, Trump has alternated between threats of escalation against Iran and indicating he could wind down hostilities, with the two sides in a standoff over efforts to resolve the conflict. item.title: Foreigners continue to offload Korean stocks in Oct.
item.description: Foreign investors continued to sell Korean stocks in October amid extended geopolitical risks and woes over artificial intelligence (AI) profitability, data showed Friday. Offshore investors offloaded a net 25.97 trillion won ($19.49 billion) worth of local stocks last month compared with a net selling of 19.11 trillion won the previous month, according to the data from the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS). Following their net selling in October, offshore investors owned 1,899 trillion won worth of local stocks, or 34 percent of total market capitalization. By country, investors from the United States were the top sellers in October by selling a net 15.9 trillion won, followed by Asian countries with 5.6 trillion won of selling, the latest findings showed. In the local bond market, foreign investors purchased a net 7.63 trillion won worth of local debt last month. Their holdings of Korean bonds stood at 330.3 trillion won as of end-October, accounting for 11.3 percent of listed bonds here, the FSS revealed.

item.title: Producer prices drop in Oct. on lower food prices
item.description: Producer prices fell for the first time in three months in October, driven by lower prices of agricultural goods on mild weather conditions, central bank data showed Friday. The producer price index (PPI), a key gauge of future consumer inflation, dropped 0.1 percent last month from a month earlier, following a 0.1 percent on-month gain each in August and September, according to the preliminary data from the Bank of Korea (BOK). The index had risen for 10 consecutive months since September 2025 and fell in July. From a year earlier, producer prices rose 7.2 percent in October, slowing from the previous month's 7.6 percent on-year gain, the latest findings showed. Producer prices are a key indicator of future inflation trends, as they influence the prices businesses charge consumers in the months ahead. The BOK said prices of agricultural, livestock and fisheries products declined 8.3 percent in October due to increased supply of fruit amid good weather and decreased demand for pork after the Chuseok holiday in September. item.title: China exposure set to widen profit gap among Korean tire makers
item.description: Korea’s three tire makers — Hankook Tire, Kumho Tire and Nexen Tire — are set to see their European profit margins come under pressure, as the European Union (EU) tightens trade barriers on tires manufactured in China as early as next month. The EU is expected to finalize countervailing duties on Chinese-made tires in early December, posing an additional financial burden to Korean tire makers after the EU started imposing anti-dumping duties from July. If finalized as currently proposed, the combined tariff rate on tires made at Chinese plants and exported to Europe will rise to 28.76 percent both for Kumho Tire and Nexen Tire, and 27.5 percent for Hankook Tire. The impact will vary widely because the three companies rely on Chinese plants to different degrees for their European sales. About 50 percent of Kumho Tire’s European sales are supplied from China, compared with around 30 percent for Hankook Tire and only about 4 percent for Nexen Tire. item.title: Kia salesman turns 32 years of local ties into 4,000-car milestone
item.description: For Kia's senior auto consultant Cho Doo-hwan, years of building relationships across the local community have helped him earn a rare distinction — selling 4,000 vehicles over his career and joining the automaker’s ranks of elite salespeople. Over 32 years, he has focused on establishing a strong customer network through local organizations, school ties, community activities and even volunteer work — relationships that have helped him achieve the sales milestone just months before retirement. item.title: [WEEKENDER] Next chapter of Korean instant noodles: Beyond Buldak
item.description: Global consumer hits such as Buldak and Shin Ramyun have demonstrated new possibilities for Korean instant noodles, showing that products once thought to be only for Korean consumers can whet appetites overseas as well. As demand for their products surges outside Korea, reflected in rising export volumes, food companies are beginning to reorganize their production bases and product portfolios to sustain the momentum and cater to global consumers. Their strategies center on two main goals: expanding production capacity and offering a wider range of products beyond the intensely spicy varieties that have helped drive their global popularity. Samyang Foods, which introduced Buldak in 2012, expects to complete and begin operating its new manufacturing plant in Jiaxing, Zhejiang province, China, by the end of this year. item.title: [WEEKENDER] How Korean instant noodles conquered world
item.description: In the monster movie “Kraken,” which premiered in Norwegian theaters in February before opening in other markets, a character played by Mikkel Bratt Silset is seen looking out over a fjord while slurping a bowl of Buldak instant noodles in the remote seaside village of Vangsnes. Another scene shows Nongshim's Shin Ramyun cup noodles inside a grocery store in the village, reflecting the everyday presence of the popular snack well outside its nation of origin. Korean instant noodles gained even wider exposure in Netflix's “KPop Demon Hunters,” which became a global sensation last year. The film, which garnered more than 600 million views in 2025 alone, making it the most-watched original film and title in the platform's history, features members of fictional K-pop girl group Huntrix eating what appear to be Shin Ramyun cup noodles. In the American Netflix series “The Brothers Sun,” which premiered in 2024, a deputy district attorney in Los Angeles played by Highdee Kuan is seen pouring seasoning powder from a Buldak packet over crushed dry noodles, enjoying it as finger food.

item.description: Experts warned that the two-state approach gaining ground in both Koreas could entrench the peninsula’s division, calling instead for a unification strategy focused on freedom and human rights for North Koreans, backed by deterrence and the alliance with the United States. Citizens’ Solidarity for One Korea held the 2026 One Korea Strategy Forum at the Korea Press Center in central Seoul’s Jung district, Nov. 10, under the theme “The Two-State Trap and One Korea.” The organization was founded in February to counter the two-state approach and campaigns for a unified Korea. At issue is a framing the government itself has adopted: the Lee Jae Myung administration has made peaceful coexistence its central North Korea policy and its 2026 unification white paper described inter-Korean relations as a peaceful two-state relationship. Hong Yang-ho, the forum’s moderator and a former vice unification minister, said North Korean leader Kim Jong-un shocked South Koreans in 2023 when he declared the two Koreas hostile states foreign to each other, effectively renouncing unification. item.title: Beyond apologies: Korean adoptees, families renew calls for government accountability
item.description: Overseas Korean adoptees, Korean birth families and civil society organizations gathered outside Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul Oct. 30, calling on the government to address decades of human rights violations and family separations linked to intercountry adoption. The press conference brought together overseas adoptee organizations and Korean advocacy groups in a united effort to seek accountability for past adoption practices and their lasting consequences for both adoptees sent abroad and families who remained in Korea. The gathering came more than a year after President Lee Jae Myung apologized to overseas adoptees and their birth families in October 2025, following the findings by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) of systemic human rights violations in Korea's overseas adoption practices. Despite apologies and kind words given toward those whose rights have been violated by international adoption, those who gathered at Cheong Wa Dae argued that official acknowledgment has yet to result in meaningful assistance or accountability. Choi Hyung-suk, head of Korean Unwed Mothers Family

item.title: Gold hits 14-month low as strong dollar, rate bets weigh
item.description: Gold fell more than 1 percent to a 14-month low on Thursday, as it continued to face pressure from dollar strength, with markets fully pricing in a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting owing to stubborn inflation. Spot gold was down 1.3 percent at $3,674.13 per ounce by 2:05 p.m. ET (1905 GMT), after touching its lowest level since September 2025 at $3,667.19 earlier in the session. US gold futures for December delivery settled 1.5 percent lower at $3,685.50. "Interest rate expectations and a strong dollar are two factors weighing on gold prices today. Minutes from last month's FOMC meeting showed almost all Fed officials expected interest rates will need to move higher, and inflation data released since that meeting support further rate increases here in the US," said Chris Gaffney, head of World Markets at EverBank. The dollar index this week reached its highest level since April 2025, making greenback-priced gold more expensive for overseas buyers. item.title: What to know about Anthropic's massive IPO as it breaks records on Wall Street
item.description: A little-known Silicon Valley startup working just a few years ago, Anthropic, the maker of the popular Claude chatbot, went public in a record-setting stock listing. As it has grown into a giant in the booming artificial intelligence industry, Anthropic has also sprinted ahead of rival OpenAI in the race to sell shares to investors. At the start of trading Thursday, Anthropic's valuation leaped to $2.01 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record. Here is what to know about the initial public offering. item.title: Wall St slides as Anthropic's debut fails to revive AI trade optimism
item.description: U.S. stock indexes tumbled on Thursday after Anthropic's blockbuster market debut failed to ease concerns about the AI trade, triggering a broader market selloff. Shares of the AI lab briefly soared past $2 trillion in market valuation, but pared gains and was last trading up 15 percent around $95.50. The company priced its upsized offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising $81 billion in the largest listing on record. "It has failed to rekindle enthusiasm for tech stocks," said Joe Maher, market economist at Capital Economics, London. "We wouldn't read too much into the expected initial 'pop' in Anthropic's share price as a stock's early trading tends to be noisy." The listing follows weeks of selling in chipmakers and cloud companies as investors fretted over stretched valuations, heavy spending on AI infrastructure and the fallout from the abrupt exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Amazon fell 2.7 percent while Alphabet ticked down 0.6 percent. Both are among the biggest investors in the AI lab. "It's difficult to draw conclusions from the first

item.title: From tarmac to APEC summit table, Japan's PM cuts a lonely figure
item.description: SHENZHEN, China/TOKYO — From her arrival in China without the fanfare that greeted other world leaders to her seat near the end of a summit table, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi cut an isolated figure at the two-day APEC gathering. Takaichi arrived at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Wednesday on her first visit to China since triggering a dispute with President Xi Jinping last year by saying an attack on Taiwan could prompt a military response if it also threatened Japan's survival. The row took an economic turn, with Beijing, Japan's biggest trading partner, curbing exports of critical minerals used in everything from cars and computer chips to jet engines. When asked at a press conference on Thursday whether Japan would intervene in a conflict over Taiwan, Takaichi declined to answer what she called a hypothetical question. "There has been no change whatsoever" to the position Japan set out on Taiwan in 1972, she said. item.title: Trump bought up to $265,000 of Nvidia stock in September, disclosure shows
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump bought as much as $265,000 in Nvidia stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of the stock in September, weeks before reports surfaced of CEO Jensen Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy, according to Trump's latest financial disclosure released on Thursday. U.S. lawmakers have been asking questions about Trump's knowledge of Huang's personal life, and the president has said he "was amazed" by the allegations against Huang, who is among the president's closest allies in Silicon Valley. Trump administration officials are currently weighing policies that could shape Nvidia's future, including rules governing exports of its advanced chips. Nvidia faces heightened scrutiny after news reports surfaced that Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman accused of spying for Beijing. Reuters has not independently confirmed that the woman is a spy. The Nvidia trades were among hundreds the president made in September, according to the disclosure signed by Trump on November 1 and made public by the U.S. Office of Government Ethics on Thursday. In August

item.title: Anthropic tops SpaceX with record $2 trillion Nasdaq debut
item.description: Anthropic notched a valuation of about $2 trillion in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, vaulting past SpaceX's massive June listing and capping a turbulent stretch for the AI sector that tested Wall Street's appetite for the technology. The early exuberance, however, partly faded, signaling volatility ahead as investors locked in quick gains and the main indexes retreated amid renewed jitters over the sector's outlook. Shares of the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company opened at $111.5, 34 percent higher than the IPO price of $83. But the stock pared its gains and was last trading around $99. The AI euphoria has somewhat cooled in recent weeks, marked by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's exit, but now shifts Wall Street's spotlight on to its rival OpenAI as the industry's next major public listing. "We like the enterprise AI narrative, but we do not like overpaying for market sentiment. It isn't a prudent 'buy-at-any-price' opportunity for retail wealth clients," said Talley Leger, chief market strategist at The Wealth Consulting Group. "History shows that retail investors buying hot tec

item.title: Takeaways from the historic summit between Trump, Xi and Putin
item.description: SHENZHEN, China — The meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin on Thursday was the first-ever sit-down for the leaders of the three countries. They started with talk of a shared responsibility for keeping peace as the victors of World War II and as global powers. But post-meeting readouts by the three nations reflected more symbolism than substance. The “peace declaration” released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran. It said they agreed on the need for reforms to the United Nations, on increasing oil supplies and on reducing nuclear risks. The statement did not spell out the type and extent of the U.N. reforms the leaders agreed to. The three sides also agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, opposing what they called “jurisdiction abuse” by the International Criminal Court, the reports said. Here are key takeaways from the talks, which lasted over an hour. China's Xi presided over the summit of 21st century powers Xi added to China’s alread

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin release 'peace declaration' from unprecedented summit
item.description: SHENZHEN, China — Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed on a symbolic "peace declaration" at an unprecedented three-way summit on Thursday and reaffirmed that nuclear war should never be fought, but announced no plans for arms control talks long sought by Trump. A joint declaration released by the world's three biggest nuclear powers capped a three-day diplomatic swing by Trump through Asia that produced few tangible victories, despite his repeated boasts about making history and brokering peace. Instead, the trip raised fresh questions among US allies about his increasingly close relationships with Xi, and with Putin, who continues to wage war with Ukraine. The powers "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and added that they would "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation of nuclear weapons," without giving a time frame. But the statement made no mention of any negotiations on a trilateral nuclear arms reduction treaty, something Trump has pushed since hi

item.description:
Stephen ‘Steve’ D. Shockey, 59, died Oct. 19 at Honokaa Hospital. Born in Texas, he was a talented carpenter, a beloved father and a cherished friend. Private family services will be held. Survived by Daphane Panui of Kapaa; son, Justin Panui-Shockey of Honolulu; daughter, Leilia Panui of Bellevue, Wash.; father, Gerald Shockey; sisters, Sarah (Joe) Williams and Sharon (Richard) Davis, all of Texas. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary, Inc. – Hilo Branch.

item.title: Newly established Opioid and Substance Abuse Council holds first meeting
item.description:
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The inaugural meeting of the newly established Opioid and Substance Abuse Council (OSAC) was convened last Friday by Governor Pulaaliʻi Nikolao Pula and Lieutenant Governor Pulumataala Ae Ae Jr. at the Governor's Office in Malaeoletalu, Fagatogo.

The meeting brought together government officials, healthcare professionals, law enforcement representatives, religious leaders, and community stakeholders to confront what many consider one of American Samoa's most pressing public health and public safety challenges.

The event also marked the beginning of a long-overdue coordinated effort to develop long-term strategies aimed at reducing substance abuse, strengthening treatment and recovery services, and preventing illegal drugs from reaching the Territory.

Representatives from the Office of the Attorney General, the Department of Health, Department of Public Safety (DPS), Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and several community organizations participated in discussions focused on the effective use of opioid settlement funds and the creation of a comprehensive territory-wide response to substance abuse.

Officials described the council as a vehicle for bringing together agencies and community partners that have often worked independently on related issues. The goal is to improve coordination, share information, and ensure resources are directed toward programs that produce measurable results.

A significant portion of the discussion centered on efforts to curb the introduction of illegal drugs into American Samoa, particularly through ports of entry and the U.S. Postal Service. Council members stressed that reducing the local availability of illicit substances must remain a cornerstone of the Territory's anti-drug strategy.

The issue takes on added importance following changes in territorial law enacted by the Fono last year. Under the new law, responsibility for investigating and enforcing drug smuggling cases intercepted at seaports, the airport, and through the postal system has largely shifted from the Department of Public Safety (DPS) to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Previously, DPS served as the lead agency in nearly all drug interdiction cases. The legislative change was intended to strengthen border security efforts by placing greater responsibility on DHS, whose mission includes protecting the Territory's borders and points of entry.

However, questions remain regarding the Territory's readiness to address emerging threats, particularly the possibility of fentanyl reaching American Samoa.

During a Senate hearing last month, Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean questioned Homeland Security Director Vaetagaloa Glenn Lefiti about the department's preparedness to prevent fentanyl and other dangerous narcotics from entering the Territory. 

In response, Vaetagaloa acknowledged that DHS currently lacks some of the resources necessary to effectively combat the threat, noting that additional funding, equipment, and personnel would be needed to fully carry out the department's expanded enforcement responsibilities.

The concerns raised during that hearing highlighted the importance of close cooperation among law enforcement agencies, health officials, and policymakers as the Territory seeks to strengthen its defenses against increasingly sophisticated drug trafficking operations. The concerns were also raised with Governor Pulaali'i during his October 14, 2026 press conference. In response, the Governor explained that shortly after his administration took office in 2025, DHS Director Vaetagaloa approached him seeking American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding to support the department's operations.

Governor Pulaali'i said he learned that during the tenure of former DHS director, the late Samana Semo Ve'ave'a, the department had received little to no financial assistance. He noted that this situation came to light four years after American Samoa received ARPA funding from the federal government in 2021.

“As a result, I allocated $8 million from our office's ARPA funds to DHS,” Governor Pulaali'i said. “The department used the money to construct an access road to Mount Alava, allowing personnel to more easily reach the antennas and other communications equipment located there. The project was intended to help ensure uninterrupted communications with the U.S. DHS and other relevant agencies throughout the mainland United States and the Pacific region.”

However, the Governor noted that the project sparked disagreement with the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA). According to Pulaali'i, ASTCA's director maintained that matters involving telecommunications infrastructure fall under the authority's jurisdiction, raising questions about whether the project should have been overseen by the local DHS or ASTCA.

During Friday's meeting, council members emphasized that enforcement alone cannot solve the problem. Participants agreed that prevention, education, treatment, and rehabilitation must play equally important roles in any long-term solution.

One initiative highlighted during the meeting was the Department of Health's ARPA-funded Drug Rehabilitation Facility, which is currently under construction. Once completed, the facility is expected to provide much-needed local treatment services for individuals struggling with addiction, reducing the need for families to send loved ones off-island for care and recovery.

(Samoa News should point out that the drug rehabilitation facility project is facing possible funding problems if the use of ARPA funds is not extended from its current December 31, 2026 deadline. The project is seeking an extension to May 2027.)

Members also discussed the importance of improving data-sharing among government agencies to better identify trends, track drug-related incidents, and coordinate responses. Enhanced communication between health professionals, educators, law enforcement officers, and community organizations was identified as essential for early intervention and effective prevention efforts.

To support these goals, the council established specialized working groups that will focus on public education, prevention programs, treatment services, and community outreach. Particular emphasis will be placed on reaching young people through schools, churches, youth organizations, and village-based programs designed to raise awareness of the dangers associated with drug use and addiction.

Governor Pulaali'i and Lt. Gov. Pulu emphasized that lasting success will require the active participation of the entire community. They encouraged churches, village leaders, nonprofit organizations, and families to become partners in the effort to protect future generations from the devastating consequences of substance abuse.

The newly appointed members of the Opioid and Substance Abuse Council include Assistant Attorney General Louise H. Lafitaga; Deputy Commissioner of DPS Lauti Tautalasoʻo Moliga; Department of Health psychiatrist Dr. Peni Biukoto; DHS Director Vaetagaloa; Deputy Treasurer Levi Reese; clinical psychologist Dr. Jueta (Eta) B. McCutchan; Reverend Iasepi Ulu; and community representative Ipu Lefiti.

The council is expected to meet regularly as it develops policies and recommendations aimed at creating a safer, healthier, and drug-free American Samoa.

Council members stressed that reducing the local availability of illicit substances must remain a cornerstone of the Territory's anti-drug strategy.
The issue takes on added importance following changes in territorial law enacted by the Fono last year. Under the new law, responsibility for investigating and enforcing drug smuggling cases intercepted at seaports, the airport, and through the postal system has largely shifted from the Department of Public Safety (DPS) to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Previously, DPS served as the lead agency in nearly all drug interdiction cases. The legislative change was intended to strengthen border security efforts by placing greater responsibility on DHS, whose mission includes protecting the Territory's borders and points of entry.
However, questions remain regarding the Territory's readiness to address emerging threats, particularly the possibility of fentanyl reaching American Samoa.
During a Senate hearing last month, Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean questioned Homeland Security Director Vaetagaloa Glenn Lefiti about the department's preparedness to prevent fentanyl and other dangerous narcotics from entering the Territory.
In response, Vaetagaloa acknowledged that DHS currently lacks some of the resources necessary to effectively combat the threat, noting that additional funding, equipment, and personnel would be needed to fully carry out the department's expanded enforcement responsibilities.
The concerns raised during that hearing highlighted the importance of close cooperation among law enforcement agencies, health officials, and policymakers as the Territory seeks to strengthen its defenses against increasingly sophisticated drug trafficking operations. The concerns were also raised with Governor Pulaali'i during his October 14, 2026 press conference. In response, the Governor explained that shortly after his administration took office in 2025, DHS Director Vaetagaloa approached him seeking American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding to support the department's operations.
Governor Pulaali'i said he learned that during the tenure of former DHS director, the late Samana Semo Ve'ave'a, the department had received little to no financial assistance. He noted that this situation came to light four years after American Samoa received ARPA funding from the federal government in 2021.
“As a result, I allocated $8 million from our office's ARPA funds to DHS,” Governor Pulaali'i said. “The department used the money to construct an access road to Mount Alava, allowing personnel to more easily reach the antennas and other communications equipment located there. The project was intended to help ensure uninterrupted communications with the U.S. DHS and other relevant agencies throughout the mainland United States and the Pacific region.”
However, the Governor noted that the project sparked disagreement with the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA). According to Pulaali'i, ASTCA's director maintained that matters involving telecommunications infrastructure fall under the authority's jurisdiction, raising questions about whether the project should have been overseen by the local DHS or ASTCA.
During Friday's meeting, council members emphasized that enforcement alone cannot solve the problem. Participants agreed that prevention, education, treatment, and rehabilitation must play equally important roles in any long-term solution.
One initiative highlighted during the meeting was the Department of Health's ARPA-funded Drug Rehabilitation Facility, which is currently under construction. Once completed, the facility is expected to provide much-needed local treatment services for individuals struggling with addiction, reducing the need for families to send loved ones off-island for care and recovery.
(Samoa News should point out that the drug rehabilitation facility project is facing possible funding problems if the use of ARPA funds is not extended from its current December 31, 2026 deadline. The project is seeking an extension to May 2027.)
Members also discussed the importance of improving data-sharing among government agencies to better identify trends, track drug-related incidents, and coordinate responses. Enhanced communication between health professionals, educators, law enforcement officers, and community organizations was identified as essential for early intervention and effective prevention efforts.
To support these goals, the council established specialized working groups that will focus on public education, prevention programs, treatment services, and community outreach. Particular emphasis will be placed on reaching young people through schools, churches, youth organizations, and village-based programs designed to raise awareness of the dangers associated with drug use and addiction.
Governor Pulaali'i and Lt. Gov. Pulu emphasized that lasting success will require the active participation of the entire community. They encouraged churches, village leaders, nonprofit organizations, and families to become partners in the effort to protect future generations from the devastating consequences of substance abuse.
The newly appointed members of the Opioid and Substance Abuse Council include Assistant Attorney General Louise H. Lafitaga; Deputy Commissioner of DPS Lauti Tautalasoʻo Moliga; Department of Health psychiatrist Dr. Peni Biukoto; DHS Director Vaetagaloa; Deputy Treasurer Levi Reese; clinical psychologist Dr. Jueta (Eta) B. McCutchan; Reverend Iasepi Ulu; and community representative Ipu Lefiti.
The council is expected to meet regularly as it develops policies and recommendations aimed at creating a safer, healthier, and drug-free American Samoa.
